Term, she reit as though she woula drop to the ground. Yet, with great control, she set her face and tapped at the door. It was opened by Cor- nelius Ildirehin, a tallish, sturdy man of about forty years, with just a few streaks of grey in the hair above his temples. His face was fresh and ruddy, and his eyes of a light blue. He seemed surprised at this visit from Mercy ; btu he bade her come into the sitting-room and, with a rather shy manner, he sat down before her the window recess.

"A long time since you were at the farm," be said. " I hope things are going well with you ?" Without looking at him, Mercy said: " Cor- nelius' do you still care for me ?" His eyes opened wide, and there was a deeper tinge of red on his cheeks. "Same as ever, Mercy, every bit the same," lie answered wonderingly. _ _

" Then I /reckon I've changed. my mind," she said, looking up. " What ! you do love me. after all? " I don't know for certain whether I do . I've not given the matter a deal of thought sine,. you last asked me. Maybe, I might come to I), very fond of you, Cornelius, and maybe I mightn't. 'Tis a risk for both of us. ." I'm prepared to run it," he svid eagerly. " I shouldn't wonder now if you're not a main :sigh: fonder o' me than you care to own to. Net as I ever set myself rip to he much of a catch for any woman. But, Mercy, honour. bright, I always did say to myself, ." If there's one woman in Bradhembnry for me 'tis Mercy Sanders.' And all along I've kep' a-hatkicerin'Ans that idea, like a sorter dream as might conic true after all. When I heard that yam brother John was Ong to marry, says I, • NOWPB your opportoonity, Cor-. nelius Mirehin, for one more last and final pro- posal to Mercy.' Well, them two other refusals that you give me was terrible hard to bear, and you may be able to understand that I've flinched and held back, not from any change o' feeling, mark you, but for fear of a third and finalest re- fusal. But now you come, as open as daylight. and welcome as flowers in May, gnd meet me fair with the very question as ra have given all I own for you to ask me ! I take it as this is Providence and that we was ordained for out, mother all along." He took her hand, and con- tinued : "You're put it to me so honest, Mercy. SISTER _MERCY,
GEOFFREY MORTIMER (Author of " Stars o' Destiny," fe.)

When John Sanders had finished Ms short Per- ,:ice with the Devon regiment, be went back Bmdhembury—where his father had been game- keeper,—and applied for the post of river bailiff to the Tivvy Conservators. AS bis character was good, and his knowledge of the habits of salmon exceptional. John obtained the appointment out of twenty-five candidates. At that time his sis- ter Mercy was keeping a small general shop over against the Blue Lion Inn, and John was glad to make a home with her. Mercy's shop VMS down two steps, and it had a half-door, to which a noisy bell was attached on the inner aide. Be- hind the dusty window panes was a quaint vari- ety of wares, and at a glance in passing you saw -a few dried onions, a box of herrings, a heap of slay marbles, and two or three penny tin whistles. Over the door was a jay in a wicker cage, and at the sight of Mercy the bird flapped its wings, and cried " Yack, Yack !"

_ Now John and Mercy were left orphans when the boy was sixteen and the girl twelve, and they bad clung together in their loneliness, and grown to sympathise one with the other more deeply and devotedly than the ordinary brother end sis- ter, so that folk often remarked upon their affec- tion as a somewhat uncommon spectacle and a "" touching " one. While John wits working as under-gardener over at Ashlington, and during his term of soldiering, he wrote often to Mercy, and now and again he sent her postal orders, with which she might purchase ribbons and such like to brighten herself up on Sundays; for Aunt Amelia, with whom the girl lived at the little shop, was not able to allow pocket money to her niece. At the death of old Miss Matthews, Mercy became the proprietor of the shop, mid upon its prueeeds, and occasional assistance from her 1:1..;b,.;-, she continued to live. i ny young, doting wife ever knew as i:elight in cooking and mending for a husband, as Mercy Sunders experienced in keep- ing bons,- for her brother. It was like a flood of sunshine lot into the house to have John back again in the village, arid under her roof of lone- some winter nights. He was so natty and order- ly, too, after his service with the colours, that he proved a most valuable helpmate in domestic matters.
"A nicer man about the house there couldn't be," said Mercy to the postmistress over the way. " fie's all so handy as a woman, and, I will say, tidier than me, all on account of hisaoldier life."

" Knowing' what plagues the men ;an be, as I do well," returned Mrs. Hood, " I'd thank God on my banded knees for such a house-follow as your John. As I was only saying last evening to Mrs. Bywater, • Mercy Sanders' brother John is better than any linsbancl as ever breathed.' "I do believe that you're right, Mrs. Hood. And what's more, me and John get along to- gether a precious deal smoother than any mar- ried couple as I can call to mind. A kinder heart than John's isn't to be found in Bradhein bury." "What a pity 'twill be when be sets his affec- tions on another woman," remarked Mrs. Hood reflectively. •• You'll have to prepare yourself against that, Mercy." A shadow seemed to cross Mercy's face and her lips winced slightly. She had thought of such a happening. and the thought had hurt eer with a keen anticipatory pain. John was the only one of her kin in England : the two other brothers had emigrated to America years ago. The presentiment that she might lose John, that another woman might become part of his life, and thrice dearer to him than the most tenderly loved sistet could frier be, brought a choking feeling in bar throat, and a mist before her eyes. She had never been in love, though two honest fellows had sought her. All her woman's affec- tion was centred upon the tall, handsome soldier brother, who had never been far away from her. thought at any time since the days when they toddled hand in hand to make daisy chains it. Long Mead. The hope of his return at the end of his service had been a constant solace. How happy she would be to have him sitting by the fire, smoking his pipe as father used to do in the old days when they were children! It was eight months now since the hope was fulfilled, and no trouble bad shadowed the home. Why should fate send a minx to steal away her dear John? For as sure as sunrise, the woman who could captivate so good a man would be a minx or a hussy. Was it not always the way ? The best men were the easiest victims of the bold, design- ing women.

Reasoning thus to herself, Mercy resolved to guard her brother against the wiles of the en- chantress, exaggerating a suspicion of peril into an immediate and palpable danger. Was it not probable that Mrs. Hood knew more than she eared to say? Mercy arrayed the spinsters of Bradhernhury one by one in her mind. 'Un- doubtedly, Lettice Amory had a way of glancing under her eyelids at John, as he walked up the aisle of the church on Sunday mornings. And if Lettiee was above suspicion, how was it that she so often came to the shop at hours when she knew that John was usually at home ? A few months ago' Lett ice never entered the shop, but now she had developed a ta,te for lollipops and a quits on wonted solicit utl; concerning the state of Morey Semler.' health. That Mercy could read the lit Ils flirt lihe a hook

" Well, let her try her best," !alio said smil- ing "sli&ll dud more than her twitch in me ! If John ma rric,l a butterfly creature like that, it woold torsi my hair grey." In church, on hituisyt Mercy kept her side glsnee fixeil upon Leitice during the sermon, ard she Fm.metitnem contrived to sit so that " that girl of Amory 's " eoula not catch a view of John's face without leaning forward in her pew. The fear that. Let lice was entleaveuring to win John's admiration approached morbidity in Mercy's mind, when he chanced to say one day that Fer- nier Amory's -daughter had one of the sweetest. and good tempered smiles be had ever seen ou a maid's face. " As if Lettice don't know how to look her best in comp'ey," said Mercy. •6 But those who the prettiest out walking is often the ories who keen their black looks and. tantrums for home. never been a manageable girl to her parents, and they sty that she's terrible quarrel. come with her sitters."

div.head: Daresbury Petty Sessions
div.p: Daresbury Petty Sessions
TUBSDAY.—Before Messrs. J. C. Parr (chairman), W. Long, John White and H. Neild.

ORTIELTY TO A MARE.—John Campbell and John Helps, both of Salford, were summoned for cruelty to a mare on the towing path of the canal at Latchford Without, on the 25th February, the former by beating it with a whip and the latter by working it while it was in an unfit state.—P.C. Williams said the mare was drawing 27 tons of manure and was in a terrible condi- tion, and quite unfit for work. Its bones were nearly protruding through the skin. Inspector Gibson corro- borated, and said the horse was not fit for work of any kind, and should be destroyed. It bore marks of hav- ing been severely thrashed.—Campbell admitted striking the mare once with a knotted whip.—Helps was tined V. and costs, and Campbell was discharged with a cau- tion.

div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
Wycliffe. P.S.A. Society.

- The second meeting in the new year of this prosperous society was held in Wycliffe church on Sunday afternoon when Mr. H. P. Densham, of Orford, presided over a good attendance and spoke upon "Let your light so shine." He said good and careful example was what all ought to aim at—example at work by punctualty and attentiveness. The employers, on their side should be considerate, encouraging and fair. He asked his bearers to be thoughtful in all things and to be righteous, whether seen or unseen, remembering that God saw and had full knowledge of all their ways. Mr. Robinson of Manchester yoke upon "Be not deceived," or" Right sowing," As they sowed their seed whether good or bad—so would their harvestbe. Therefore let them live good, happy, and useful lives. The secretary welcomed fifteen new members. He briefly referred to the trouble and inconvenience experienced by their chairman owing to the fire at Orford and expressed the sympathy of the meeting with him. Heannounced that about 380 prizes had been obtained during the last six months and would be distributed next Sunday afternoon. Mr. William Miles and Mr. A. Healey also took part in the Meeting. Mr. Payton presided at the organ. Mr. Hale was the soloist. Buckley Street P.S.A. Society. • -

There was a large congregation at an open-meeting of the above society on Sunday, and in the unavoidable absence of Mr. A. H. Crosfield, the gathering was pre- sided over by Mr. C. Jackson Holmes. A brief address was given by the chairman, after which the Lyric Prize Quartette (Misses A. Woodland, L. Fairhurst, and Messrs. R. Cook and I'. George) gave a sweet rendering of " God is a spirit." Miss L. Plinston was heard to gread advantage in her solo, "Queen of angels." The solos " Ora pro nobis "and " The Holy City ' by Miss W. Cox and Master A. Cox were well given. Miss L. Fairhurst, gave a fine rendering of "The raft" with which she was successful in winning the first prize at the St. Helens Eisteddfod. Miss M. Plinston and Mr. A. Trow were the accompanists. At the close of the musical part of the programme Mrs. Jackson Holmes presented half yearly prizes to about 150 members. Thirty-six new members were enrolled on Sunday, making a total of 186 OR the register. The Welsh Revival.

Scenes at the Welsh Revival formed the subject of the sermon delivered at the Bewsey-road Wesleyan Church, on Sunday morning, by the Rev. R. Wilkins Rees. While on a visit to Cardiff a few weeks ago, Mr. Rees visited several revival centres, and on Sunday he gave a very interesting and impressive description of what he saw and experienced. He referred to the orderly manner in which the meetings were conducted, and said that no undue influence or emotion was brought to bear upon the congregation, but the place seemed filled with a divine power. Some very touching incidents were narrated, but, best of all, the rfAival, like all true revivals, affected the morals of the people ; old debts were being paid, persons who had not been on speaking terms for years had become reconciled, and

M. Dienert, in a note to the Academy of Sciences, Paris, states that powdered magnesium destroys the microbe of typhoid fever, bacillus coli, and the bacillus of Eberth.

Dr. Voigt suggests that what are called volcanic craters in the moon may be the coral islands or atolls of a lunar sea now dried. The Pacific Ocean, if evaporated, would, he says, leave mountains resembling volcanic craters.

The "piesnic " barometer of Mr. A. S. Davis consists of a glass tube 71n. long, bent like a syphon, but one leg longer and thicker than the other. The long leg dips into mercury, and the indications, though not fine enough for scientific purposes, may serve for a weather prediction.

div.head: PLANETARY ROTATION PERIODS.
div.p: PLANETARY ROTATION PERIODS.

The period of rotation of the planet Mercury has been variously estimated, by means of spots on the surface, at twenty-four hours or more. Schiapa- relli, however, maintained that, like the moon and the planet Venus, its next-door neighbour, Mercury, rotated round its axis in the same time as it revolved round its primary, so that it always presents one face to the latter. He gave the period as eighty-eight day ss: According to an observation of Mr. M`Harg, the period is twenty-four hours and five to eight minutes. As Schiaparelli seems to be right in the case of Venus, and seeing his great reputation, the question cannot be taken as quite settled yet.

div.head: NEOMYLODON.
div.p: THE NEOMYLODON.

The neomylodon is a strange animal of the Tertiary period in geology, whose remains have hitherto been found in Patagonia by Nordenskj old and others. The remains are chiefly fragments of the skin found in caves, apparently the dens of the beast. It is not known whether the neomylodon is quite extinct or not, and it may be that survivals will be found either in Patagonia or elsewhere in South America. A fresh contribution to the subject has been made by Dr. Capitan, who has presented to the Academy of Sciences, Paris, a piece of its skin found in the cave of Cueva, Argentina, along with other relics of the animal in a More or less fossilised state. The skin bears long white silky hairs.

div.head: PHOTOGRAPHY THROUGH A PIN-HOLE.
div.p: PHOTOGRAPHY THROUGH A PIN-HOLE.

Professor Gregory, in the Leisure Hour, tells us how to set about this interesting experiment. Make a minute hole in a card, with the point of a pin or needle, and hold the card between the flame of a candle and a piece of white paper or card. An inverted image of the flame will be seen upon this screen, and its size will depend upon the relative distances of the pin-hole from the flame and screen. A small aperture behaves, in fact, like a lens, and for some purposes it is better to use a pin-hole can era than the usual camera with a lens. With an ordinary camera, it is necessary to focus the object upon the screen; but with a pin-hole camera no focussing is required, the definition of the image being the same at all distances from the aperture.

div.head: IS DEATH PAINFUL?
div.p: IS DEATH PAINFUL?

The immediate cause of death, in all but very exceptional cases, such as accident, is the poison- ing of the nervous centres by carbonic acid, which accumulates in the blood owing to the failure of the arrangements for its removal. This gas, let us mark, is an anfesthetic, and has, indeed, been employed as such, both locally and otherwise. This property of carbonic acid may be termed, says Dr. Saleeby in the Academy, "a merciful provision of Nature." Normal death, if the phrase be per- mitted, is a painless occurrence, usually preceded by gradual loss of consciousness entailing no more suffering than going to sleep. The accumulation of this merciful gas often induces muscular contrac- tions or spasms, which are preceded by loss of consciousness, but may have suggested to un- critical observers that their moribund subject was in "agony." It is not merely that the pain of death is trifling as compared with the physcial pain of a scald: it is non-existent.

div.head: TREES IN WIRELESS TELEGRAPHY.
div.p: TREES IN WIRELESS TELEGRAPHY.

Major Squire, of the fI.S. Signal Corps, • has made experiments at Fort Mason, California, with growing trees as antennte and " earths " in wireless telegraphy, and finds them serve the purpose. Instead of earthing 's wire, it is enough to drive a nail into a tree some two inches above the ground and connect the wire to it. The tree itself can also act as an antenna or air-wire, a fact useful in military field telegraphy. Mr. Frederick Collins. in the O'cientific American, has described the Major2s method of using the tree for an air-wire. It is based on the well-known observation that if a vertical wire earthed at its lower end is one-fourth the wave length of the received signal waves, the ceest of the waves of current and the node of the waves of potential in the antenme are at or near the earth line. The Major, therefore, connects the apparatus for telegraphing, namely, the transmitter or receiver, at the base of the tree. One terminal of the apparatus is connected to the base of the tree at the ground, and the other terminal to the earth itself at a distance from the tree of one-fourth of a wave-length. A branch of the signal currents thus passes through the apparatus and wits to earth, and makes the signals.

MOTORIST TO PAY £5O. An Oldham Man Run Down and Severely Injured.
At the Oldham County Court, Arthur William Stig- wood, a weighing machine maker, of 59, Alfred-street, Oldham, was awarded ,C5O compensation for injuries he had received in a motor-car accident.

It appears that the plaintiff was crossing the road to board a tramcar. The " motor " came along at about fifteen miles a hour, and swerved suddenly when near the car, crashing into Mr. Stigwood and a friend. The former was rendered unconscious, and in this state was taken to the Oldham Royal Infirmary suffering from a compound fracture of the left leg and a broken shoulder.

Though the bones " set" and he was walking about on crutches in 10 weeks' time, the doctors feared some permanent disablement. The affected limbs continued so stiff and sore that he had the greatest difficulty in getting about and was unable to go to work. While in this condition he chanced to try Zam-Buk, which has now completely restored to his arm and leg their former suppleness and strength. "When 1 got out of bed for the first time after the accident," said Mr. Stigwood, " I felt as if I should be a cripple for life. Even though I had crutches, it was difficult and sometimes positively painful to move my joints or have any strain put upon my limbs. I des- paired of ever again being able to work. My shoulder • was so bad that I could barely reach up to my ear with my hand, even when dropping my head sideways aslow as I possibly could, and it was as much as I could do to get the crutch under my arm, the stiffness made me so helpless. One day a small sample of Zam-Buk was thrown in at the front door, and I rubbed the balm occasionally on my arm, which was quite stiff from the elbow to the shoulder. To my great surprise and satisfaction I found that by the time I had finished the sample I could lift my arm higher. I decided to persevere and obtained a large box, and when I had finished this I could raise my arm over my head. Zam-Buk seemed to penetrate right down into the tissues, and to give the muscles new life and strength like no embrocation could have done. I got alfurther large box, and rubbed the balm in regu- larly. Now the numbness and the stiff, cramped feeling has entirely disappeared. To-day, added Mr. Stigwood, suiting action to word, "I can reach as high as ever I could. I can lift ahundred-weight with this arm with case. Whilst lam testing my machines it is all weight- lifting, and I can do this just as comfortably as I did before I met with the accident.

"When the plaster mould was removed from my leg the ankle was very sore as well as stiff. I thought that what Zam-Buk had done for the shoulder it would do for the ankle, and I commenced rubbing it in. The effect was wonderful; and now, thanks to Zam-Buk, the skin is healthy, and I am free from lameness, and as active as I was before the accident. I have great faith in Zam-Bnk." Because of its unique Zam-Buk is superior to old style embrocations. It is Nature's own balm for skin, flesh and muscles. div.p: LITERARY AND PHILOSOPHICAL
SOCIETY.
Annual Meeting.

There was a large attendance at the annual meeting of the above Society which was held in the Masonic Hall on Monday evening. Mr. F. G. Ruddock presided. Mr. ROBERT DORSON hon. secretary, presented hie annual report, which showed there was an increase in the number of members. The lectures during the session had, he said, been most interesting and instructive, and under the guidance of the President everything had passed off successfully. Mr. RUDDOCK, in moving the adoption of the report, said it was a matter for congratulation that they were making so much progress in view of the many counter attractions in the town. (Hear, hear.) Mr. J. RYMER Yotree seconded, and the report was adopted. Mr. A. J. JOLLEY proposed the election of Alderman Bennett as president of the society for the coming year. He thought the interests of the society cculd not be put into safer hands. (Applause.) Mr. Ruddock would become vice-president in accordance with custom. He also proposed that Messrs. J. Rymer Young and Josiah Longland be elected on the Council of the society in place of Mr. Burgess and Colonel Buckton, who retired; that Mr. Dobson be re-elected hon. secretary, and Mr Sileock, hon. treasurer.
The Rev. G. VALE OWEN seconded, and the motion was carried.

Alderman BENNETT returned thanks, and said he keenly appreciated the honour they had done him. On the motion of Mr. J. RYMER YOUNG, seconded by the Rev. C. HARVEY COOK, Mr. Ruddock was thanked for, services as president during the past two years. Mr. RITDDOCK replied and expressed thanks to the retiring - members of the Council, the Hon. Secretary and Treasurer, and Mr. Sutton the lanternist. Mr. Woonnuen, lecturer in biology at Huddersfield Technical College, then gave a lecture on "Woodland plants." He explained where the various woodland plants were to be found, the circumstances of their growth, and how they were'affected by their surround- ings. The lecture was illustrated by lime light photo- graphs, the lantern being manipulated by Mr. Sutton. At the close Mr. Woodhead was cordially thanked, on the motion of Mr. CH ARLES WRITE, seconded by Mr. Jolley.

div.head: LOT OF A LONDON TAILORESS.
div.p: THE LOT OF A LONDON TAILORESS.
A Side-Light On An Important Subject.

The following letter, written by a London tailoresS, is interesting as showing the hardships which some members of this class have to undergo, and the boon which bile beans prove in illness. It is typical of scores of letters received daily by the proprietors of this great vegetable specific : King Street, Regent Street, London. Gentlemen, Some time ago I was troubled with chronic) constipa- tion and an acute pain in my side, both being due to liver disorder. Often the pain was so bad I could hardlylie in bed. A friend advised me to go to the Middlesex Hospital, and I did. After iveeks of treatment, however, I could see no improvement, so I ceased to attend. I am a tailoress, and as I have to work from eight in the morn- ing to eight at night, you may guess what misery I endured.

Seeing in the paper an account of a case like mine which had been cured by bile beans, I told a friend of mine that I thought of trying them. She had tried them, and said, "Do! I'll buy you the first box ! " I commenced with them, and they soon cured the constipation. It was not, however, until I had finished the second box that I felt what a wonderful change bile beans had made.

For the first time for a long period I felt really hungry, and enjoyed the heartiest meals day by day without any ill-effects afterwards. Then the headache ceased, the bodily pains went also, and I found I was cured. Bile beans have done me more good than I ever believed possible. Gratefully yours, MABEL CLEGG. The reputation of the medicine so highly spoken of by Miss Clegg is built on a sure foundation, for bile beans through their general excellence have now become the leading' family medicine. They are purely vegetable in composition, and suitable for the most delicate con- stitution. They cure cobstipation, headache, dizziness, wind, pain after food, biliousness, female ailments, blood impurities, debility, anzemia, and all liver and kidney disorders. Obtainable from all chemists at one and three-half-pence or two and nine per box. You should be careful to avoid substitutes and imitations, and also any prepa.ration like bile beans in appearance, but sold in loose in pennyworths.

A Lesson From Warrington. The Mayor (Alderman • S. Quinn) presided over the monthly meeting of the Widnes Town Council on Tuesday.—Mr. Boyle said he would like to draw attention to an item On the minntes, which related to an account of lls. for safety-pins,for Calvert Limited. He had made inquiry, and found that Mr. Lewis, a member of the Council on the Finance and Health Committees, was a partner in the firm. He protested against such doings, because he knew it was wrong, and it ought to be the duty of everyone to keep their name spotless. Recent affairs at Warrington ought to teach them a lesson,because one never knew where such matters would end. Other business was of an extremely quiet nature, the whole proceedings only lasting fifty minutes.

Queen Victoria's Granddaughter.—lt is hoped that Princess Margaret of Connaught will, like Princess Charles of Denmark, spend much of her time in this country, after her marriage with Prince Gustavus of Sweden. The Prince's father—the Crown Prince of Sweden, is only forty-seven years of age, so that in the ordinary course of life it will probably be many years before Princess Margaret will be called upon to play the Part of Queen of Norway and Sweden. If we except Princess Charles of Denmark, there are only three of the late Queen Victoria's granddaughters who have their homes in this country, namely, the Duch ,ss of Fife, Princess Louise of Schleswig-Holstein, and Princess Alexandra of Teck. Twelve have married and reside abroad, whilst six are unmarried. These are the Princess Victoria, the Princesses Margaret and Patricia of Con- naught, Princess Beatrice of Saxe-Coburg, Princess Victoria of Schleswig Holstein, and the d‘butante Princess Ena of Battenberg. The late Queen Victoria saw much of Princess Margaret and her sister, in their childhood, as the Duke and Duchess of Connaught, were then a great deal abroad, and their children to a great extent were left in charge of their grandmother. The Swedish Royal Family. There are several marriage relationships between the Royal Families of Sweden and Denmark. Queen Alexandra's niece Princess Ingehoro is married to Prince Charles of Sweden,and our Queen's sister-in-law the Crown Princess of Denmark, is a neice of King Oscar. Neither the Ring and Queen, or the Crown Prince and Princess of Sweden have any daughters. Prince Gustav Adolphus Who is to married Princess Margaret of Connaught, has two younger brothers, the youngest being an artist of recopised talent, and unmarried. The Swedish Royal Family belong to the Lutheran Church, in which the Duchess of Connaught who is a Prussian, was also brought up. Concerning Weddings.—There has been quite a rush of society weddings lately, as is usual just before Lent. That of Lady Magheramorne and the Hon. Hugo Baring was particularly charming, quiet affair though it was, and the same may be said of Sir Stephen Gattv's marriage with Miss Katharine Morrison at St. Peter's, Eaton Square. Miss Morrison wore some very beautiful moonstone and diamond ornaments, and Sir Stephen Getty presented the bridesmaids with brooches composed of the same gems. There is quite a craze for moonstones at the moment, and in every fashionable bride's collection of gifts some ornaments containing them, are in evidence. Princess Henry of Pless.—lt is hard to realise that more than thirteen years have passed since the much- talked of wedding of Prince Henry XV. of Pleas and Miss Daisy Cornwallis West, for the Princess has ?stained all her girlish beauty, and at the christening 'of her little son the other day looked not one day older than she did on that memorable occasion in 1891. Tall and willowy of figure, she has an exquisitely fair com- plexion, blue eyes, and a wealth of true golden hair, moreover she thoroughly understands the art of dress. White and pale blue are the Princess's favourite wear, and she has a great affection for turquoise ornaments. Her elder son, now five years of age is a fine healthy 1407, who does credit to his powerful sponsors, King -calward and the Kaiser. The baby Count who was given no less than seven names, has received very hand- 'some presents f rem Queen Alexandra, who stood as god- mother, the Prince of Wales who stood as godfather, and the German Crown Prince, and Mr. George Corn- Vrallis West, who were the other sponsors. The Royal Yachting Trip.—The Queen, with Princess Victoria, and Prince and Princess Charles of Denmark, Will, it is hoped, have an enjoyable holiday cruise in the Mediterranean. The health of Princess -Victoria is the primary object in view, but the Queen has never 'before visited Portugal,and she gave a promise to do so When Queen Amtilie had to curtail her recent visit here. on account of the illness of her sister, the Duchess of Aosta. Many people who have wintered on the Medi- terranean shores this season have complained a good deal of the continuous cold weather there. It has been said, and not without truth, that one needs a cast iron constitution to be able to winter on the Riviera, but better weather should favour the Royal Yachting trip at this time of year.—No fixed route or plans have been f ormed, but random calls will be made at places which seem most interesting at the time. The cruise will last about two weeks, and early next month the Queen and Princesses will land at some b...editerranean port, and proceed to Copenhagen, before the birthday of the aged King of Denmark on April Bth. The Mistress of the Robes--The Duchess of Bum- leach is understood to be desirous of resigning the office of mistress of the Robes. The appointment singularly enough, is a political one, subject to a change of ministry, but it is rumoured in Court circles that she Will In succeeded by her sister-in-law, the Duchess of Abercorn. The Duke and Duchess of Abercorn have both held various Court appointments and are on terms of intimate friendship with the King and Queen. His lVfajesty having, as Prince of Voiles, stood sponsor to the marquis of Hamilton, the Duke's eldest son and heir. The Duchess of Bucclench is one of the several daughters of that venerable lady, the Dowager Duchess Of Abercorn, who might be said to be the mother of the peerage. She has been the Mistress of the Robes both to Queen Victoria, and to Queen Alexandra,having held this office since the year 1885, except for a brief interval in 1886, and from 1892 to 1895. The Ducal Aliansions.—The Duke and Duchess of zlarlborough intend to give a magnificent ball at Sunderland House after Easter. This is their new London residence where there was recently a small .euse-warming entertainment, on which occasion the n-hlg and Queen honoured the Duke and Duchess with their presence at dinner. Hitherto the Duke, who is tOS ninth holder of the family honours, has been with- out a town house worthy of his rank and position, but .1,10 expense has been spared in the building of Sunder- land House, and he now possesses one of the finest mansions in London. When the Duke married the great American heiress Miss Consuelo Vanderbilt, he hoped to be able ti re-acquire Marlborough House, the resid- !nee of the Prince,of Wales ,i but as this was impossible, " began the building of his new home, which is named ter one of his subordinate titles, the Earl of Sunder- land. The Duke of Roxburghe, who also -aarried a great American heiress, Miss May Goelet, intends to follow the example of his cousin, the Duke of Marl- borough, in building a new ducal mansion. He too is Without a town house of any note, and is now engaged in looking for a suitable site on which to indulge his housebuilding fancies. Cheating at Bridge.—One hears a 4od deal about eating at bridge, and those people who have so much gay about the wickedness and hollowness of modern Ll,e, generally go on to assert that women are muoh t'wre addicted to this vice than are men. It is quite impossible to say whether this is so. or not, as those who make a general attack of this kind seldom take Pains to verify their sources of information, and as a rule such denunciations come from those who never had `'ca lt,rd in their hands in their lives. At the same time Cre is no doubt, more cheating at cards in the aggregate since bridge has become the universal amusement of all °lassos. The game lends itself more readily to this :lean vice than whist, and sons other games, since it is ° easY for one player to indicate by unnoticeable signs. what he or she wishes "declared." This means pre- arranged plans, to which of course, no decent people syould stoop, and the wholesale allegations that present calY society is given over to such vices, may be dis- Missed as ridiculous exaggerations.

div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

• About Colours.—The idea of choosing a colour—the most becoming of course—and remaining faithful to it, has found much favour with exclusive dressers, for several seasons past, but so far the woman with the small dreas allowanee to whom the notion would make for decided economy, will have none of it. This is a state of affairs to deplore, as the amount saved in the matter of accessories where one colour is worn to the exclusion of all others is almost incredible. Pale blue has many advocates, 'Lady Lansdowne favours it, so also does Lady de Trafford, and the young daughter of Lord and Lady Arthur Hill. Mauve has many friends, partly no doubt on account of its extreme becoming- ness, though unquestionably its popularity has much to do with Queen Alexandra's preference for this particular hue. Green has fewer supporters: despite the fact that it is this spring being offered us in the most exquisite and entrancing shades. The fact is that the average British complexion is not set off by green, and save by the leading Irish beauties, it is comparatively little worn. Orange has its devotees, among them Lady Cynthia Graham, Miss Muriel Wilson, Lady Ulrica Baring, and Lady Alington. Grey and black appeal to many leaders of fashion, Lady Algernon Gordon- Lennox being devoted to the latter, also Lady Hindlys, who as a debutante appeared very frequently in all black•toilettes. The Popularity of Lilac.—ln the artificial flower world, lilac reigns supreme, milliners and dressmakers being agreed as to its perfections. And truly this bloom is perfect, a miracle of artistic achievement. So far the idea this season seems to have been to copy Nature exactly in form, and run riot in colour, but in , colour and form alike the lilac is perfect, and to carry out its realism it usually exhales the natural perfume. I Queer Pocket.—With the departure of the pouched bodice and the pouched sleeve, we are rendered desperate our last apologies in the way of a pocket having vanished. The underskirt pocket is a failure of which we are all convinced, but the new idea of a garter pocket seems likely to prove more so. The round stocking supporter in chiffon, ribbon, or lace is fitted with a purse, and several tiny pockets,while the one below the suspender is finished with a chiffon flower, from which depends several buds' each bud containing some item ; such as a very small handkerchief a miniature powder puff, a bag of rice, a wee mirror, a sachet, a purse. eto., I etc. In the first place, the same objection obtains to the garter pockets as to those set in the frills of the ; underskirts, namely the impossibility of getting to. them with any degree of gracefulness, and secondly, all ! those little accessories dangling about the knees do not make for comfort. This is absolutely devoid of decoration or trimming of any kind, and is worn round the neck with one long end hanging down and the other thrown over the left shoulder. The fashion simple though it is, is a costly one, for so perishable a material cannot be made to do duty twice. More simple styles.—We have been indulging in a craze of checks, both large and small, and in • more or less impossible colorings. Taken altogether we should do well to avoid checks, save those very small ones which become invisible at a little distance. In teffetas glace silk, these tiny checks afford to the surface of the fabric a dainty shot effect, which is particularly charm- ing. Tailors however, are preferring the plain fine cloths, and these are in the palest shades, and made up in the simplest possible styles. The full sleeve, the leading tailor refuses to build, preferring the neat coat and skirt variety, which follows quite closely the line of the arm, and is in harmony with other equally severe outlines of the fashionable coat and skirt. Modish Colors.—The vogue for brown dies hard, and the new shade of pale cinnamon will, in all probability, enjoy a great vogue. This delightful colour lends itself admirably to those little touches of pale green, or turquoise blue, so much in favour among dressmakers and milliners, this spring, and owing to a certain amount of pink in its composition, it will prove ex- ceedingly becoming to the generality of women. As is usual when Lent comes round, every shade of mauve ana lilac are in evidence, also delicate tones of lavender and silver grey. White and cream are more worn than ever before, the woman with the moderate dress allow-

Legh-street Band of Hope. On Tuesday the fifth popular entertainment in con nection with the Band of Hope Society was given in the Legh-street Sunday school. As usual an admir- able programme was gone through. Mr. G. Whileld was responsible for two excellent recitations which were highly appreciated. Songs were given by Miss Elsie Hayes, Miss Ruth Boardman the Misses Clare and Ada Titchett, and the Misses Kathleen Cole, and E. Millington, delighted the audience with a character song entitled " Gay little girls from Japan." Missegi Cole and Millington were also responsible for violin solos and duets which were tastefully executed. Miss Turner's well-known ladies' orchestra was a great attraction and won warm applause from the audience with pleasing selections which were highly creditable to their capable conductor. Miss Turner also favoured the company with a mandoline solo and was accom- panied by Miss Burke who also pli.yed the accom- paniments for the orchestra. R,ecitations were given by Miss Ethel Shaw, Master Ted Edwards, and Miss ,Nellie Fitton, pianoforte solo by Master Percy Smith, I and Miss May Isherwood assisted by a juvenile party, gave a character song entitled "Call to the Flowers," in a most pleasing manner. The chair was taken by Mr. Joseph Bissell and the accompanist for the even- ing was Miss Annie Titchett. Dialogues were also given under the leadership of Mr. W. Dale. Altogether the performance was most interesting and enjoyable throughout and it must be highly gratifying to the promoter Mr. H. Billingbam that his efforts are so much appreciated by the large concourse of friends who invariably assemble at his well-known concerts

div.head: CHEAPEST GAS IN THE KINGDOM.
div.p: CHEAPEST GAS IN THE KINGDOM.

Sir P. T. Mappin,M.P., was unable through indisposi- tion to preside at the meeting of shareholders of the Sheffield Gas Company on Monday. The chair was taken by Mr. Wilson Mappin, who said that the consumption of gas had increased from 1,258 million cubic feet in 1884 to 2,745 million cubic feet in 1904. The price had gone down from 2s. 2d. per 1,000 cubic feet an 1901 to 1. 2d. per 1,000 cubic feet at the end of this quarter— the lowest price in the kingdom. At Ipswich on Thursday a married woman named Cann was sent to prison for a month in the second division for cruelty to a three-year-old child, one of Dr. Bannardo's waifs. The evidence showed that defendant thrashed the child unmercifully and burnt it with a hot flatiron. The marriage of Signor Marconi to the Hon. Beatrice O'Brien,daughter of Ellen Lady Inclaiquin, was solemn- ised on Thursday afternoon at St. George's, Hanover Square, London, in the presence of a large and distin- guished congregation. The public greeted the bride- groom with rousing cheers. A German newspaper publisher was reoently fined for giving a quarter of a column of space to the advertise- ment of a patent medicine, on the ground that to give so much space was " bombastic " and irritated the reader.

The reign of silk among us is universal. At all times of day, and in every kind of gown, it is seen on the greater proportion of well-dressed women in the West-End. The favourite,*ays a Globe writer, is taffetas, but a thin, dull silk of not too flexible quality is also used a great deal, particularly for morning dresses. Shepherd's plaid and tartans are much favoured for these plainer frocks, and they make up very smartly indeed. Flat pleats, not so full as the accordion and sun-ray pleating of a month or so L back, are the most effective. The tartans are, of course, dark, and even those in which the subdued colours are relieved by a slight line of white are apt to be a little glaring in appearance, or at least unbecoming to the figure.

ance having discovered that in these days of quick and inexpensive dry-cleaning, the mode is by no means as expensive as it would appear. An Old-Fashion Revived.—White linen collars and cuffs, embroidered or plain, are being prepared to wee with linen gowns, the majority of the collars being very high, and the cuffs deep. Coloured embroidered linen cuffs, collars and belts may also be had, and so wide is the choice in tones that it will prove an easy task to match a gown.

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.
THE WOUNDED ST. HELENS POLICEMAN.

Police-constable H owells, of the County Constabulary, who was shot and terribly stabbed by a poacher at St. Helens on Monday night, February 27 is, we are! glad to know, almost out of danger, though weak and in pain. Police-constable Adams, of the St. Helens force, who was shot the same night,is now able to get about at the hospital, and is doing well. ST. HELENS POSTMASTERSHIP.

Mr. C. C. R. Twist on Wednesday vacated the position of Postmaster of St. Helens and left the town to take up his new duties at Maidenhead, Mr. A. H. Hender- son, assistant surveyor, of Liverpool, is taking temporary charge at St. Melens, and Mr. T. Batten has been appointed chief clerk in succession to Mr. S. H. Tranter. A movement has been set on foot to recognise Mr. Twist's services to the town. * ATTEMPTED SUICIDE.

Ernest Turner, of Hall-street, was charged at St Helens, on Thursday, with attempted suicide. Mr. Ellerington, chief constable, said that until recently Turner was apprentice to Mr. Henry Smith, hairdresser, of 2, Liverpool-road. On Friday morning, the 24th ult., Mr. Smith's son heard groans at the back of the shop, and found Turner leaning over a table with his throat cut and a razor in his right hand. He had since been in the hospital.—Turner was handed over to his father who promised to look after him.

Lady Ilelen•Vincent once had a grey velvil wt!: big sleeves of white muslin, covered. with ,TeRlll Lady de Grey has been seen wcarit.::: ;_rf,y diii on, brightened by the gleaming red of ii r )tiLks ; and at the first February Court Lady Lansdowne appeared in a poetic costume of grey vetet, with a cream lace train, and her 'wonderful pearls to complete the symphony in neutral colourings. Soft grey woollens have a decided attraction. Charming combinations of grey, black, and white can be arranged both for day and evening dresses. One of our cleverest dressmakers—an artist in colour—made a dinner- gown in grey and black chiffon, with the bath and sleeve ruffles of cream-shaded Irish lace. A SPRING COSTITME.

Though still experiencing somewhat wintry weather, we are, in reality, on the verge of the spring season, and a spring costume will soon become a necessity. Such a costume, both smart and useful, is depicted in our sketch. The material used is a fine dark blue cloth. The coat, =Me with stitched shoulder capes, has open revere, which, together with the crossed vest, are fashioned of glossy cream cloth beautifully embroideeed

soft greens and blues and a touch of dull gel*, while the buttons are green stones set In a surow band of dull gold. The skirt is perfectly plain except for the tiny piped pleats down the front, and the belt is of very soft blue leather. A hat of blue straw, trimmed with an immense rosette of blue silk, having as centre a very large button similar to those on the .coat, completes the costume.

div.head: FASHIONS IN FROCKS.
div.p: FASHIONS IN FROCKS.
SM&RT BLOUSE.

The subject of our sketch is a smart little blouse in spotted saie-de-cliine, The triple-puffed sleeves reach only a little way below the bend of the elbow, where they end in rounded tucked cuffs of plain fileusseline-de-soie edged with narrow lace. Ruche*

of tbla same lace conceal the fastenings down the front, and the collars are of lace-edged mousseline to match the cliffs. A bright note of colour is added in the original way in which straps of cerise ribbon are brought down from under the collars and bunched up into rosettes at the bend of the figure, while this colour is repeated in the broad belt of flexible kid. TAXINII PIANOFORTES.

There are certainly some things they manage better in Germany than in England. The munici• pality of one of the German provinces has just decided to impose a tax of ten marks on every separate possessor of a pianoforte in each house- hold. This certainly ought to have some deterrent effect upon merciless piano-bangers reckless of other people's n( ryes. In these days of loosely run up houses and flat-life, such a tax in England might possibly bring us some measure of relief.

div.head: LENT IN WENT LONDON.
div.p: LENT IN WENT LONDON.

Every milliner's shop is displaying Lenten purple and violet. Some of the most fashionable West-End houses have windows entirely filled with gowns in the various shades of these colours. A remarkably pretty hat seen the other day was of white fancy straw, with the brim turned up in front, and entirely covered with pale purple and white wood violets, arranged in broad bands. A loosely tied bunch of violets and their leaves gave the necessary height at the left side. A larger hat as made of mauve crinoline straw, and had a semi-transparent effect. A small bunch of mauve roses caught jn the brim near the front, and another bunch decorated the bark. TO-DAY'S RECIPE.

DRESIMi Parrins.—Cut three slices of stale bread about Ilia. thick; then stamp out rounds with a plain a ttter about 3in. in diameter. Hollow out .the centre of each, leaving a case of bread. Cut a neat little round top to fit each case. Dip the cases for a few seconds in milk; then drain them. Chop Cool': ilb. of cold meat, one small onion, and enough to fill two teaspoonfuls of parsley. Mix these all together; add a little gravy or sauce, and salt and pepper to taste. Next brush the cases of bread over with beaten egg and cover them with bread- crumbs; then fry them a golden brown in boiling fat. Make the meat-mixture hot; fill in the case, piling the mixture rather high. Put on the lids after frying them, and serve them hot, garnished with fried parsley.

Bad men however have usually a considerable sense of humour and also pretty tough skins, and a letter of incoherent abuse from some reli- gious faddist or half deranged person may be as spiteful as he pleases but it is only on that account the more amusing, and if the skulking enemy has an idea that his letter will be treated as a jest he is apt to be discouraged. When your critic has packed all the nasty adjectives he could select into one letter of four pages, and it is read aloud at the breakfast table for the refresh- ment of a hilarious family who ought to have been saddened b), the names their afflicted father had been called, it is hardly worth the trouble of sending the letter. And somehow this tribe of sharpshooters get an idea of the men who are easily hit and the men to whom the most venomous assault only brightens the morning hour. It is a rule with the wordly wise I have heard, that every letter which is not signed be put without reading it into the fire, and in this way the recipient will escape a great deal of annoyance. No doubt this is so if he be a morbidly sensitive man, but if he be a humor- ous person he will miss many an hour of simple enjoyment. Another class which affords much unworldly pleasure to a' properly constituted mind is the letter writer who is not in the legal sense insane, and could not 'be put in an asylum, but who is to use an excellent Scots word, distinctly "daft." Very likely we are all daft at some point, and would give forth a very remarkable sound if the particular note were struck, btit fortunately the unstrong wire is at an extreme end of the key-board and is therefore, with most of us, very seldom touched, but with our leas fortu- ate friends it is a note in the very middle. As it is only a single note their fingers can keep off it during practical business. It is quite likely that our daft correspondent may be a careful book-keeper or a tax-paying householder, and talk quite sensibly on the weather, and see that he gets the proper change out of a sover- eign. But let the note be touched and off he goes. A clerical Mend of mine, and in this matter clergymen have singular privileges, has been receiving at intervals for the last five years letters from a produce merchant on what may be called current topics in the other world. Some- times they are messages sent through this cor- respondent to the clergymen about doctrine and duty, sometimes they are pieces of interest- ing information, and it may be a layman's point of view, but when I have had the privilege of reading the letters, the information was more interesting, and certainly fresher that the dogma which seemed to show that the revision of creeds had not made the progress one could have de- sired on the other side. But the news came with all the pleasure of a surprise. As, for Instance, to take only one of the latest dispatches, that while other languages are understood on the other side and may be used by the less for- tunate nations, for ntcessary.p.urposes English is

DROWNED IN A POND. James Egan, the two-year-old son of James Egan, bootmaker, Widnes-road, Widnes, was drowned on Tuesday in a pond off Milton-road He went out to play in that direction, and was away for a while, when an alarm was given and a young man named Hogan got him out. Dr. Edwards was sent for, and respiration was tried by the doctor, Constables Cleal, Moseley, and Howard, but without avail. The affair caused a sensa- tion in the neighbourhood. WIFE'S DISAPPEARANCE AT RUNCORN. On Monday night the wife of Harry Parkes, well. sinker, of Bentinck-street, Runcorn, did not return home. On Tuesday morning Parkes received by post a letter from us wife, bidding him "Good-bye for ever." She said she had "threatened to do it "many times, but he was "now rid of her." She asked him to be good to the lads. It is supposed the woman has committed suicide. The letter was posted at Runcorn at 9.15 p.m. on Monday. RUNCORN URBAN DISTRICT COUNCIL ELECTION. In three wards the retiring members are returned unopposed—Halton, Mr. F. Wiswall, C.E.; Mersey, Mr. Tom Jones; Heath, Mr. James Pritchard. In Central, Mr. Ellis Gatley is opposed by Mr. T. Kennedy, grocer; Bridgewater, Mr. W. Handley is opposed by Mr. John Littler' quarry owner, and in Newtown, Messrs. W. Carroll and Matthew Thomas are nominated against Mr. Sam Walton. DEATH OF A WIDNES NEWSPAPER PROPRIETOR. .

Mr. Thomas S. Swale died On—wnaw-i4iiqsa.his residence, Highiield-road, Widnes.—The deceased served his time as a printer in Liverpool, and afterwards migrated to Birkenhead. Subsequently he enlisted in the Hussars, and was drafted to India, where be saw active service,and remained there some time. Upon his return to England be came to Widnes, and commenced to work at the Widnes Foundry. Later he set up a printing works, adjacent to Victoria-road, in Croft-st., and on January 1, thirty years ago, published the first copy of the "Widnes Weekly News." Runcorn slid Garston editions were added shortly after in the order named.—He was a member of the Institute of Journal- ists. During the whole of his residence at Widnes he was prominently associated with the Victoria-road Wesleyan Chapel, and a class leader in the Lacey-street Sunday schools; and the temperance movement found in time a powerful advocate.—About eight months ago he was actively engaged in the management of the business, when he was obliged to relinquish his work on the ground of ill-health. Forsome time he was entirely absent from the office, and whilst away he was unfor- tunate to lose the whole of his premises and plant by fire. From then until a week ago he took an active part In the restoration, and practically died in harness.—He lci s a widow and family to mourn his loss, and a large number of the townspeople will regret the sad loss Widnes has sustained.

One's correspondence, if at all extensive. is a .lal mirror of human nature, and looking there- in he meets with many interesting and amusing, and sometimes painful people. For 'instance there is the anonymous letter writer, and by that one means, not the person who does not sign his name, but the person who refrains from signing his name because he wishes to say unpleasant things. As regards the pleasant bat anonymous letter, and this is not at all uncommon, one only wishes that ,the corres- pondent who has done his best to cheer a writ- ing man or clergyman by some encouraging words had only revealed himself, for such letters have often been to weary men as a brook by the way, and have deserved a grateful reply. I shall always remember one note which caused the sun to shine upon_ me when the sky had been grq. and it was signed "twenty-one." Twenty-me • will now be twenty-six I caleulate, but in the time between I do not think she (for the writer was a young woman) can have done many more human and cordial things than the writing of that letter. Yet I shall never know who "twenty-one" is, and she will never know that she helped a lame dog over a stile.

Anonymous however Inis an evil sound and is generally associated with letters which state your faults in a frank, stmighforward laid which not infrequently convey the meaning in simple soldierly language, without any fast- idious restraint of charity or delicacy. What such correspondents say is occasionally true, although generally untrue, but it is alway- written wider a constraining sense of duty, and is as disagreeable •as the ability of the person can Make it. Abuse may be either stupid or clever, and everyone cannot scarrify you with skill. Sensitive men suffer immensely from this attack at long distance range, because they cannot see their foes, and have no chance of replying. One of • the most pious and devoted clergymen i have ever met had bundles of . anonymous letters in a drawer of his writing table close to his hand, which he seemed to preserve as a kind of a hair shirt for his very inconsiderable sins and one could see that the friction chastened his soul. What the people wrote to him about strained one's • curiosity, for he was orthodox to the last degree, maintained a puritan standard of conduct, ard occupied his spare time with meetings on the conversion of the Jews. But 'I imaigne .the letter writers were maiden ladies of a, certain Age whom, he had disappointed by his marriage, for out of all the crowd that circled round him he could only marry one, and it was rather surprising he married any; or they' were re- ligious faddists from whom he. differed on some burning .question like " the Millenniun." My observation of life goes to prove that the good man suffers Much more at the hands of the anonymous brigand than the bad man, which adds another detail to the ancient problem why the unrighteous go free. In this case I hazard an explanation. The good man has usually no sense of 'humour but very tender feelings, and therefore when some slightly malignant or half crazy person writes a letter 'denouncing his views or accusing him of some absrud offence, he is much concerned. He can- not do his work, and flies signals of distress upon 'his face till his wife reminds him of their marriage vows and beseeches him to confide in her, after which a trembling voice reads the letter and the wife responds with floods of tears ; "that any man (although she suspects it is a cat of a woman) should have written to her James in such a cruel, and unchristian spirit." The writer, although he cannot be in that home, has a shrewd idea that the letter will rankle like a poisoned bullet in a wound, and from behind his Kopje he enjoys by imagination the torture of the wounded man and his wife, and has a Pleasant sense of revenge for some slight, that nobody knows anything about except himself, . or a difference of opinion t on some subject neither he 'nor anybody else knows anything about.

It appears, however. according to another dispatch, that the greatest kindness is to be extended to what may be called foreign peoples, for at the moment of writ- ing, a Chinaman and a Negro have been admitted to an audience with the highest Powers. It is pleasant however for the great Anglo-Saxon race to know on the most direct authority that as they are rapidly controlling this present world, the other woild is already in their hands Clergymen have wonderful privileges in this department of human nature, and one of them told me lately that he had been greatly cheered in the midst of hard work by letters on the Lost Ten Tribes of Israel. They came from a hard headed and, so far as he knew, otherwise per- fectly sane manufacturer who had made a con- siderable fortune by spinning something or other, and had retired from business to hunt up those vagrant Hebrews. The letters explained , that, unlike the quest for the North Pole, this search had been more successful, that Ephraim, MOM. and the rest of them were simply ti k the buns and W eish beetuett to be mere hangers on that King Edward was the direct decendent of King David, that the stone Jacob used as a pillow was in Westminster Abbey, and that the different counties in Eng- land could be assigned to their tribes, and the writer explained that he had just discovered that Ile was of the lineage of Gad. There were also a good many details regarding arrangement of effairs when the Ten Tribes had released themselves, and it was not obscurely hinted that there might be trouble between them and the two tribes who had not been lost. My own im- pression is that if there was to be anything like a division of real property, and if the an tribes claimed anything from the other two on fr - fr:g proni,sais, mere wow° be big black trouble. On the other hand the ten had done fairly well for themselves, and the liter seemed to take a hopeful view al the re- conciliation. It was all very fresh and threw a new light on England, but when a successful spinner prides himself on being a member of the tribe of Gad, one gets a new view of the possibi- lities of human nature.

Cheerful confidences of this kind are not how- ever the monopoly of clergymen, for in my own 1 day I have received (among other remarkable epistles) a letter from an American citizen ex- plaining that the cause of all erroneous think- ing was the denial of the great Bible truth that the earth is flat, and enclosing an essay of some fifty pages of foolscap showing that the scientific idea that the earth is a sphere is an absolutely ignorant mistake. The writer went on to say that he had a good many documents in reserve. together with some interesting models, and that he proposed on receiving my consent, p come over from New York, and put the matter before me, and through me before a deceived English people who were walking in darkness. Why I was chosen to be the medium of his interesting communication I do • not know, except that I was living in Liverpool and it was the point of arrival for the American steamers. This is not a case however where pleasure was unmixed with responsibility, and as I could not contem- plate any gentleman of this enthusiastic nature making so long a journey to see so humble a person, and as we have no accomodation of the kind necessary in our home for such enthusiasts, I hastened to answer his letter, beseeching him to put his remarkable discovery before some of the more thoughtful bodies likely to consider it, and as soon as it had received their imprimatur I would be glad to introduce it to an eager English public. And the bodies I suggested were Mrs. Eddy (although I should suppose she would prefer to be called a mind rather than a body),,the Theosophists, and the Shakers, the Latter Day Saints. The corres- pondence has at prefient ceased.

The following increased postal facilities in the dis- tricts of Stretton, Appleton and Hatton hare been sanctioned by the Postmaster General and came into effect on blonday last as under : STRETTON.—An extra house to house delivery of letters and parcels will take place at 5.15 p.m. in the village. Letters &c., for the outlying places may be had on application at the Stratton Post Office between the hours of 5.15 p.m. and 7 p.m. Later morning collections will be made from the district letter boxes including Norcott-Brook Post Office, to admit of sufficient time to reply to morning letters.

A later collection from the Appleton Thorn letter-box to enable the residents to reply to their morning correspondence. Spiritualist Sulky's Anniversary. The eighth anniversary of the Warring ton Spiritualist Society was celebrated on Sunday and Monday. The services on Sunday afternoon and evening were conducted by Mr. A. Plenderleith, of Ashton-under-Lyne, who delivered an address in the evening on " Are human life and consciousness separ- ate attributes ?" At both services he was accom- pan;ed by his eleven-year-old daughter, Jessie, who gave a number of clairvoyant descriptions, in nearly every case giving the full names. On Monday even- ing the annual congregational tea was held, which was fairly well attended. A capital entertainment was provided. Miss Turner and several members of their band opened with a selection for piano, mandolines ' and violins. "Up to date," which was capitally ren- dered. Miss Dorothy Turner was encored for a violin solo " Sacha " and Miss Turner was loudly applauded for a mandoline solo, " A dream of Paradise.' Mr. Jams Broadhurst sang with good effect "The veteran's song" and "Anchored." Mr. H. M. Ashton created great amusement by his reading of a couple of extracts from Max Adeler s works. Mrs. Hannan sang "Dear heart" with taste an was loudly applauded. Mr. and Mrs. Hannan were encored for their rendering of the duet " Life's dream is o'er,' and Mr. Hannan sang in a pleasing manner "For all eternity." Miss Ethel Chapman was loudly applauded for her piano solo, "Le desir," the test piece at the recent eisteddfod; she also officiated as accompanist to the vocalists. Mr. F. Monks presided at the piano for the remainder of the proceedings. At the close of the programme the President expressed the thanks of the committee to all who had so successfully con- tributed to the pleasure of the evening.

div.head: FETE t'A A MINER.
div.p: FETE t'A A MINER.
MARCH 18th. 1905.
Mr. BALFOUR has shuffled

THE HOOK OR his Government for the CROOK POLICY, second time without excit- ing much enthusiasm in his own party. It is decidedly humorous to find Mr. WALTER LoNd's appointment to the Irish office praised on the ground that he is married to a daughter of the late Earl of Conc. Apparently he has no other qualification for giving instructions to Sir ANTONY MACDONNELL. The positien of that official, by the way, was the subject of several very pertinent questions ad- dressed to Mr. BAwFun. The Prime Minister again endeavoured, without success to reconcile the functions-of an ordinary civil servant with the terms On which Sir ANTONY MACDONNELL I was originally appointed, not as Mr. WYNDHAM'S subordinate, but as his colleague. Mr. BALFOUR intimated, however, that the first arrangement will not continue, or that the Under-Secretary will be permitted to do nothing except by the order of the new Chief Secretary. To the question whether Sir ANTONY MACDONNELL would be removed altogether, no answer was returned. Mr. BALFOUR is well aware that he cannot satisfy his Irish Unionist supporters without sacrificing Sir ANTONY ; so we may look for a shuffle at Dublin Castle. The Minis- terial opportunities are quite in accord with Mr. BALFOUR'S idea, which is the avoidance of a bye- election at any cost. It is immaterial to him that his Chief Secretary knows nothing about Irish government, and that his President of the Board of Trade has had no experience whatever of business. It is entirely without precedent to appoint a peer to this office, and Mr. BALFOUR must have been well aware that the choice of Lord SALISBURY would offend a considerable number of his own friends. Unionists in the House of Commons did not conceal their annoyance,and the motion for the adjournment washy no means re. sented by all the members who sat behind the Prime Ministei.

The truth is that Mr. BALFOUR is reduced to makeshift dodges which weaken the Government day by day. The policy of hanging on by hook or by crook is nominally suppprted by MT. CHAMBERLAIN, but be does not pre- tend to like it. He and his follow,ers make no secret of their impatience. Scarcely a day passes now without some new peril for this ricketty Ministry, in which appointments are regulated, not by fitness, but by the necessity of not giving another constituency the chance of rejecting the Ministerial candidate. The Board of Trade goes to Lord SA LISBURY merely because he has no elec- tors to satisfy. The office might manifestly have, been held by a member of the lower House where he would be in contact with the chief representatives of the commercial interests. But Mr. BALFOUR is forced to set at defiance every convenience save that of a Minister who clings to office amidst the grinding weariness of his party. In spite of energetic whipping, the Government majorities are not stimulating, and the Opposition are legitimately seizing every oppor- tunity to embarrass a Cabinet which has completely lost caste. Mr. BALFOUR suggested a few days ago that the 61-eneral Election was still a long way off. It was rather an extravagant statement for a Minister who runs the risk of defeat nearly every day. He has declared that he will carry on as long as he retains a majority in the House ; but he may

be left in the lurch any moment by the apathy or Unionists who are weary of the whole business. With a dispirited army and a watchful foe, Mr. Bauroun is playing a losing game. His tactics are perceptibly less welcome to his party in the House. In the country they have failed entirely ; more than that, they have destroyed any advantage Mr. CHAMBERLAIN believes himself to have gained by his initiative. Lora L4NSD3WHE favoured the House of Lords with the assurance that nothing could be further from the thoughts and the inten- tions of the Government than an attack on Free Trade. This merely shows that they have a method of upholding Free Trade which the majority of the electors are quite unable to distinguish from hostility.

As a counter-blast to the Lloyd-George meeting our Conservative friends did a good stroke of political business in bringing Mr. A. Bonar Law to Warrington last evening. Mr. Law is one of those whirlwind orators who overwhelm opponents by a redundancy of words and figures, and in this res- pect he probably did the protectionist party excellent if temporary service. During next week we, and the public too, will have an opportunity of putting the Under Secretary's utterances to the test of analysis and logical examination. We have not met with any prolectionist arguments yet which have withstood such a test and emerged triumphant, and we are not anticipating that Mr. Boner Law made out a latter case than his two leaders Mr. Balfour and Mr. Chamberlain. By the way, it looks as if the local Conservative Associa- tion desired Mr. Bonar Law to preach only to the converted, for admission to the meeting was by ticket, whereas the opposite was the- fact in regard to the Liberal demonstra- tion. Mr i Loyd-George converted many of those whom he addressed, and it seems like a con- fession of weakness when Mr. Bonar Law is denied a similar opportunity. The fiscal question is one for the public and not for the select few, but the Protectionist orators from Mr. Chamberlain down- wards have always taken care to pack the audience with the right material for swallowing such a statement as that an excess of imports over exports spells national ruin.

The Liberal M.P.'s themselves are largely responsible for the Government having escaped defeat up to now, and the want of loyalty to the urgent needs of the party is a fault redounding to the discredit of many individuals. Had they been in their places we should probably have had a dissolution ere this, and no wonder some of the London dailies are threaten ing to pillory legislators who are so unmindful of their duty in these fateful times. Alluding to the same subject, the "Christian 1 World "says :—" Official pairs ' were refused by 1 the Liberal Whips on Monday evening, and we hope that Mr. Herbert Gladstone will have courage enough to maintain the stand he has taken. It is, however, discouraging to find that on the same evening the Tories only had a majority (and that a paltry twenty-one) through the absence unpaired, of a large number of Liberals. It would almost seem as if some Liberal Members of Parliament were in league with the Government to postpone the General Election. If constituents would whip these absentee Liberals with sharp postcard remon- strances the negligent members who are prolong- ing the life of the Government might be stirred into doing their honest duty." —We notice that the Trades Coencil has been dis- cussing the wages question as affecting Corpora- tion employes, and has endorsed the recent action of Councillor Wright. Our readers will re- member that Councillor Wright oppased all the increases of officials' salaries at the February Council meeting on the ground that many of the Corporation workmen were getting only a small wage. At the time we criticised the inconsistency of such conduct, and we are rather surprised to find the Trades Council favouring the same unen- lightened policy. As Trade Unionists they doubtless insist on a fair day's work and a fair day's pay in any branch of employment. Why then should C zporation officials be denied the increased renumeration which they have earned? Not because humbler employes are only earning a pound a week, surely ? Yet this is what the objections of Councillor Wright and the Trades Council amount to.We never heard of a more short sighted, dog-in-the-manager notion. If the members of the Trades Council are of the opinion that the Corporation dustmen and labourers are underpaid they should take steps to prove their case and obtain redress for these workers. To penalise the officials instead is a remedy which could never have been conceived in sanity and exercised in reason.

Passive fesisters have this week made what is becoming their annual sacrifice for conscience. The number of people all over the country who refuse to pay the sectarian part of the poor rate is in- creasing year by year, and the passive resisters are now an imposing body of determined upholders of freedom in thought and belief. Local resisters have appeared during the last few days at both the Warrington and Daresbury police courts,where the usual distress warrants have been issued. But the most remarkable passive resistance sale has taken place in Manchester, where the unusual 2. spectacle of a huge business concern in open :11 revolt was witnessed. The principals of Messrs. S. and J. Watts and Co., are staunch Noncon- formists; the firm is second to none in the '44' cotton goods trade and owns the largest t warehouse in the world, while the rating of the concern amounts to quite £3OOO annually. Of this a sum of £l5O was estimated as being required for sectarian purposes, and the firm resisted payment. As a sequel to the demands of the law Messrs. Watts bent some £6OO worth of goods to the aucticnee.., and the sale of these sufficed to settle the claim and all expenses. A sacrifice such as this ought to convince the most sceptical of the potency of the Nonconformist conscience.

Be road foreman. The somewhat vexed ques- tion of filling the vacancy for a road.forernan under the Corporation has taken a new aspect. In our issue of to-day we publish an advertisement from the Paving and Sewerage Committee which opens the post to fresh competition. The salary offered, it will be noticed, has been increased to £2 10s., while the qualifications remain the same. We understand that the reason for this unexpected course of events is to be found in the death of the foreman over macadam roads, the intention being to combine the two offices. Most people will, how- ever, conclude that the Committee is seeking a way out of its difficulties by making an entirely new start from a fresh point of view. It was, we think, necessary that they should !

The School Management Committee of the Education authority is making another effort to ~ obtain the free use of the second-class swimming, bath for children attending the elementary schools. A similar request a short time ago was not favour- ' ably received, but we are glad the matter is not : being allowed to dip. It is of first importance - that bathing unde4 proper conditions should be encouraged among the rising generation if for no , 'other reasons than the very pressing ones of 1 health an/I cleanliness. But if the much-desired facilities are obtained, we hope arrangements will ' be made for systematic instruction in swimming. So much has been said of late on this phas3 of the question, that it is hardly necessary now to urge it, further. Failing the provision of baths at the new: schools, the Education Committee is taking the, best course in pressing for the free use of the , Corporation baths The Town Hall, Parks, and Baths Committee would, we believe, be acting in , the best interests of the town in acceding Co the ^, request but should it remain obdurate in regard to , absolutely free use, we see no reason why the ! matter should not be satisfactorily arranged, for, as an alternative, the committee is to be invitsd ' to disclose " what fa nlities it is prepared to offg, in this connection."
For the time being, at any rite, the scheme :for the construction of a light railway betwgen War- rington and Kautsford has been abandoned. RI

div.p: face of the powerful opposition from many quarters I the promoters appeared to recognize that their case was practically hopeless and, after a long inquiry, withdrew their application for the neces- sary powers. Many people—and cyclists in Particular—who had almost feared to contemplate an unpleasant transformation of this beautiful country road, will feel greatly relieved IVe are far from being convinced that there is a real demand- for such a railway. Practically the whole of the district bordering the route is of a rural character, and very sparsely populated. By no stretch of the imagination can Knutsford be regarded as a commercial centre, and it is somewhat difficult to see how a sufficiently large volume of traffic would have been forthcom ing to make the undertaking either a valuable public asset or a commercial success.

On prima facie evidence we should say that the presiding magistrate of the Newcastle Police Court was" done brown" the other day. A prisoner charged with begging yawned nonchalantly in defence and said he wished to go to gaol for fourteen days. "We shall make the term seven days" said the magistrate with what the prisoner would no doubt coesider strange perversity. To be consistent, however, in his determination to make things awkward for the prisoner,lhe magistrate should have discharpd him. Perhaps this would have lent too much colour to the idea that the prisoner was getting the best of the bargain. At any rate, if you know your magistrate, it seems a safe plan to express a desire for imprisonment when already liable to it. Some J.P.'s would have madethe sentence in New- castle into a month,which the prisoner might have thought was overdoing a good thing. As events turned out he proved that beggars have more than an elementary knowledge of human nature.

It is a sign of the times that half-a-dozen series of the classics—two of them new this year—are being published in cloth binding at a shilling each. There is a wider public to-day for the famous books of the age than ever,since beer and tobacco canhot provide the visions that a populous library may. This fact the man with the small wage already realises. No set can hit one's taste completely ; but a selection from all should rightly contain for any reader entertainment and wisdom in such form that he is easily disposed to receive them. A course of study must ever be one of discipline ; and that, after all, is its supreme worth and one of its attractions. One need not " live with books," like Buckle, who collected 22,000 in order to write his "History of Civilisation in England." For appre- ciating the classics, it would seem, in these fortu- nate days, it is not necessary, either, to spend a competency to acquire a group of them. The working man to-day may make a list of the books he reads in a year, no less imposing than those seventeenth-century lists of Drummond and Haw- thornden. The fascination of these new and cheap issues is that one never need read more than a small proportion of them. Indeed, it is better not. The sober reader pegs out his literary claim, in time and subject, and stays upon it. Mere appetite of mind is mischievous; but that a man should light up his understanding is quite another affair. When we can do it for a whole month for a shilling, he may as well cheat oblivious night with candlelight, table-talk, and music. If a shilling be too much, there are half-a-dozen series which arrange it for sixpence. What with free, State-provided educa- tion, and the gold of literature commanded by the copper currency, the new generations should shew great advance in talent, information, and judgment upon the old.
