'Coming Events. The choir sermons will be preached at Leh-street Primitive Methodist Church to-morrow (Sunday) by -Arr. T. Tarran, Preston Brook. In the afternoon 'there will be a musical service, when the choir will render selections from "The Creation." A meknorial concert organized by the friends of the late Mr.-Percv Randall will be held in the Parr Hall On Saturday evening next. Mr. T. J. Down's orchestra -and many well known local artistes have promised their services and an attractive programme has been -arranged. Sunday, March 26th, will be observed as Hospital 'Sunday at the various places of worship in Warring- -ton, and collections will be made on behalf of the Infirmary. At Wycliffe Church to-morrow evening the Rev J°lin Yonge will preach on : " General Booth's call from Jerusalem and Dr. Horton's call from the chair of the National Free Church Council, for universal Prayer, and consecration to the service and salvation Of men" The children's annual musical drill, gymnastic •display and distribution of prizes will take place at the Gymnasium on Monday evening. The Mayoress will present the prizes.

In the evening the members of the local branch of the National Irish League held a ball in the Co-operative Hall, Winwick-street which was largely attended. Messrs. P. Frain and T. Dalton acted as and the music was supplied by Mr. J. T. Earton's band. "PREMIER" CYCLES at 12 guineas with change s'Peed gear .tc., nnequalled.—J. S. The heroic action of John Stockton, ,13, Helsby- street, in extricating the three men who were "gassed" in Ellesmere-street last week, is to be recogni sed by the Paving and Sewerage Committee, who have decided to present him with :£lO. The funeral of james Baxter at the Cemetery on Saturday was the °c'easion of a striking demonstration of sympathy, 'lnceased's fellow-workmen walking in procession. His neck Iras rather badly cut, and he at once proceeded to the 'lnfirmary where the injury was dressed. He went 'on duty later in the morning. div.head: Presentation to Mr. C. E. Place.
div.p: Presentation to Mr. C. E. Place.

Mr. C. E. Place, who is shortly leaving Warrington to take up his duties at Wakefield as markets inpector, was yesterday made the recipient of a gold pendant, subscribed by the tenants of the Warrington market. On the pendant was engraved his monogram and the words : Presented by the tenants of the Warrington market, March 17th, 1905." Mr. Atkinson made the presentation, Mr. Place suitably responding._

H. M. ASHTON'S LIFE TONIC is the KING OF TONICS.-63, SANKEY ST., WARRINGTON.—Advt. Warrington Eisteddfod Committee. At a social held at the Winmarlegh Cafe, Sankey street, on Wednesday evening the members of the above committee presented to their Chairman, Mr. Thomas Brough, a pair of silver ornaments and cake dish as a token of respect and also, in recognition of the valuable services rendered by him during the past three years. Mr. Nathan Cook made the presentation. An excellent supper was provided and a very enjoy- able evening was spent.

Drowned in a Fog. On December 23rd, John Pearson (63), 03, Cart- wright-street left his work to return home, but missed his way in the fog which prevailed, and walked into the river. Nothing further wa ; seen or heard of him until Tuesday. when his body was recovered from the river at Penketh, by P.C. Iloughton.—At the inquest, which was conducted at the Red Lion HoteLPenketha yesterday, by Mr. F. A. Jones (deputy coroner) verdict of" Accidentally drowned "was returned. Wedding at St. Paul's Church The marriage of Miss Mabel Payton, daughter of the late Mr. Wm. Payton, and Mr. Isaac Pickton, son ef the late Mr. David Pickton, was solemnized by the Rev. W. Bracecamp at St. Paul's Church on Thurs- day. The bride, who was given away by her brother, Mr. W. H. Payton, wore a dress of biscuit coloured voile trimmed with lace, and a white picture hat. She carried a bouquet of lillies and fern. The brides- maid, Miss Elizabeth Riley, carried a bouquet of xnarguerites. Mr. Godfrey Dean discharged the duties of best man. • The newly married couple left later in the day for Blackpool where the honeymoon is being spent.

UNDER THE CLOCK for Good Boors.—Advt. Mr. Lloyd-George and the Reform Club. Mr. Lloyd-George was on Thursday elected a mem- ber of the Reform Club after the heaviest poll of the Club's history. Since the Home Rule split of 1886 the Reform Club has not been of one political colour. Its membership is composed of Liberals and Liberal Unionists, who find their difference no hindrance to sociability in the Club. There was however, just a possibility that some of the Unionist Members might blackmail Mr. Lloyd-George, but the Welsh leader secured more than 00 per cent, of white balls, and was consequently elected. Hitherto Mr. Lloyd-George:has used the National Liberal as his club.
PUBLIC BENEFIT.—UNDER THE CLOCK FOR BEST BOOTS IN LANCABHIRE.—Advt.

King Edward VII. Club of Jolly Anglers. At the invitation of the vice-president, Mr. John Massey, about 39 members of the above club, sat down to a sumptuous repast at their headquarters, the Ring-o'-Bells, Wilderspool-road. A smoker was afterwards held,Mr. Macaulay being voted to the chair. Messrs. Bonnell, Boscow, Mather, Hampson, Chorley, Parr, Owen, and the Secretary contributed to the harmony of the evening. Messrs. Lawton, Shepherd and Bailey were the humorists, and were very successful in their local fishing hits. Tha usual vote of thanks brought a most enjoyable evening to a close. Ur. Thomas Boscow-, junr., was the accom- panist.
PUBLIC BENEFIT. UNDER THE CLOCK FOR BEST BOOTS IN LANCASHIRE.—Advt.

"The Air we Breathe." At the last meeting of the St. John's Literary and Social Society, Dr. Prentice, of Wilderspool, gave a highly instructive lecture on the above subject, illustrating and supplementing his explanatory remarks by a series of exceedingly interesting experi- ments. The president of the Society, the Rev. j. L. 13. D., occupied the chair, and there was a good attendance of members and their friends, who thoroughly appreciated the lecture. At the close, on the motion of Mr. Watson, a hearty and unanimous vote of thanks was accorded the lecturer for the able and instructive manner in which be had dealt with such an important and interesting subject.
LADIES' BEST GLACE BOOTS AND SHOES, UNDER CLOCK, BRIDGE-STREET.—Advt.

Innovation at the Library. An important departure has been made at the War- rington Library by the establishment of a junior section in a separate room on the right on entering the building. This section was opened for the first time on Monday afternoon and the following arrange- ments have been made for Monday, Tuesday, Wednes- day, and Friday, 4 to 7, and Saturday from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. No books will be issued on Thursday. Children 12 years old and upwards may obtain tickets entitling them to borrow books by preqenting a guarantee form filled up and signed. The innovation is supplying a long-felt want as when the junior and senior sections were combined the lending department was frequently, especially in the evening inconveni- iently crowded.

div.head: Meeting of the Stockton Heath Parochial Committee.
div.p: Meeting of the Stockton Heath Parochial Committee.

The monthly meeting of the Stockton Heath Paroch- ial Committee was held in the National schools on Thursday evening, when there were present,Messrs.G. Pilling (in the chair), Whitley, Warburton, Pearson, Fairhurst, H. J.Westbrook, T. R. Westbrook, Mclntyre, Hallows, Williams, Clarke, Ashton (clerk), Swinton (surveyor), and Farrington (inspector).—A letter was read from Mr. T. Williams with reference to the property which he is building in Old London-road. Mr. Williams said he was not aware he was breaking the bye-laws by building houses instead of shops as the houses were being so built that they could be converted into shops. He had had plans prepared which would be submitted to the committee. The letter was considered satisfactory. The tender of Mr. Thos. Stringer for (£l3 13s. 5d.) for the construction of man-holes and a sewer in Alexandra-road and Warburton-street was accepted. "PREMIER" CYCLES at 9 guineas for Best Grade. rinsurpassed.—J. S. GARLAND, 5l to 55,Bridge st.; Warrington.—Advt. Warrington Ragged School Mission. A large number of children this time over 700 were provided with a substantial tea on Monday even- ing through the generosity of Mrs. Crosfield of Conway, North Wales. Three separate sittings .were necessary, many of the children having to wait nearly two hours before they could be attended to. As each batch of the children finished their meal, they wery entertained in a upper room of the Institution with music, readings &c. A practical illustration of the distress which still prevails was shown by the num- ber of mothers who waited outside in the rain in the hope of getting a few remnants of dry bread, but they had to be disappointed, everything being eaten up by the hungry children. The exectutive of the Mission desire to express their thanks to Mrs, Crosfield for her continued interest and assistance in Ragged school work. It is to be hoped that other ladies and gentle men, who have regard for the miseries of suffering irresponsible little ones, will supplement the efforts that have already been made, in giving an occasional meal to them during the distress which still un- doubtedly exists. TO7NIC-S11:6-3. KEY:STREET, Warrington.—Advt. Good Templar Convention. The monthly meeting of the Number 1 Convention S. W. Lancashire, of the 1.0.G.T. was held on Saturday in the Old British Schools, Ashton-in.Maker- field. Bro. J. Parr, C.C.T. presided and he was sup- ported by all the executiue officers, all the lodges in the area being represented. The report of the con- vention secretary. Bro. E. Newman, reported good work being done. A good number of fraternal visits had been paid by the members to other lodges. Brighter prospects were in view at Wigan,St. Helens (where a juvenile temple was to be opened)and Widnes Hearty congratulations were passed to Bro. Houghton (Hindley), who had just celebrated his 73rd birthday and 33rd Good Templar birthday. Sister Bowler, a young member of the juveniles, who has won a silver , medal for reciting, gave a splendid interpretation of " I will paint you a sign," which was heartily received The reports of the Lodge and temple representatives were, on the whole very encouraging, and were accepted with thanks. A. special committee was appointed to revise the rules of the Convention, Bro's. Parr (Leigh), Newman (Earlestown), Merlin (Warring- ton), Punshon (St. Helens), Clarke (Earlestown), and Bowler (Ashton), being appointed. The question of opening new lodges at Sutton and Leigh was referred to the Executive Committee. The next meeting will be held at Earlestown in April.

IBewsey Ward Liberal Committee. At a well-attended meeting of the Bewsey Ward ILiberal Committee, the following officials were elected :—Chairman, Mr. Joseph Owen ; vice-chair- men, Messrs. Charles E. Bunch, Thomas Pemberton, and John A. J. Morton ; hon. secretaries, Messrs. Edwin Plinston, Charles E. W. Nurse, Horace Fear, Frederick Highley, and James Walsh. Poor Children's Summer Camp. The annual meeting of the Warrington Poor Children's Summer Camp Committee was held at the Town Hall yesterday afternoon, when there were present the Rev. Father Whittle (in the chair), Mrs. H. Roberts, Mrs. Wilkinson, Messrs. A. H. Lee (hon. treasurer), W. 11. J. Jenkins (hon. secretary), F. J. Emson and A. Malcolm, and Councillor Ashcrof t.— The Treasurer's report showed that there was a balance due to the treasurer of 14s. 10d.-,—Mr. Jenkins in his report stated that owing to the exception- ally good weather the last camp was more successful than those held in former years Two hundred and sixty boys had been taken to camp. For the first time girls had been taken to camp and the experiment had proved so successful that it was to be continued this summer. Mr. Lee said he was strongly in favour of an increased number of girls being taken to camp. The reports were adopted. The following were elected to form the general committee :—Mrs. G. Dakin, Miss Pierpoint, Mr. F. Monks, Rev. W. Bracecainp, Rev. John Yonge, Mr. J. Moore Murray, Mr. J. H. Smethurst, Mrs. Carleton, Mrs. Henry Roberts, Mr. F. W. Monks, the Rev. Father Whittle, Mr. J. W. 'Parker, Inspector Cox (N.S.P.C.C.), Mr. Hy. Taylor, Mr. G. W. Armitage, and Mrs. Wilkinson. The executive committee was appointed as follows :—Mr. J. Moore Murray, Inspector Cox, Mr. J. W. Parker, Mrs. H. Roberts, Mrs. Wilkson, Mr. G. W. Armitage, the Rev. Father Whittle and Councillor Ashcroft. Mr. Jenkins was re-elected hon. secretary, and Mr. Lee hon. treasurer.

div.head: PLEASANT TOIL FOR WORKHOUSE INMATES. The Brabazon Employment .Scheme.
div.p: PLEASANT TOIL FOR WORKHOUSE INMATES. The Brabazon Employment .Scheme.

To brighten the lives of the inmates of the Work- house Hospital by providing them with light and useful 'employment is the very commendable object of the , Brabazon Society and a splendid work in this direction lis being done in our local institution. The toivnspeople I lof Warrington werenfforded an opportunity of showing their appreciation of the scheme yesterday when the annual sale of the articles made by the inmates during the year was held in the Workhouse hospital. There was a large attendance and the event passed off very successfully. Mrs. James Fairolough, president of the Ladies' Visiting Committee, performed the opening ceremony, and amongst those present were Mr. A. .T. Jolley (who presided), the Revs. Dr. Mercer and W. Bracecamp, Mrs. Clay, Miss Broad- bent (hon. secretary), Messrs. Mather, W. Hickman, R. Forshaw, G. Thompson, S. Davies, M. W. Seton, J. Billinge, and J. F. Awbery (Workhouse master). Miss BROADBENT submitted her annual report which stated that the Matron, the Superintendent and the nurses had been most kind in helping them to get ready for the sale and had shown themselves very willing to undertake the extra work it had entailed. She had to report a year of great progress. She had a larger staff of Brabazon ladies, 14, and therefore they had been enabled to employ a larger number of inmates, but naturally their expenses had increased to a corresponding degree. They got more and more interested in the work as they saw the immense value of it in cheering the lives of the in- valids who would otherwise sit idle brooding over their sorrows. They never interfered with those who worked for the house ; the hands they employed would other- wise have been idle. Last year their lack of funds,owing to the increasing outlay in materials caused great un- easiness,but Mrs. Frost,with her her usual kindness and generosity, came to the rescue and held a sale at her house. This re tlised a sum which enabled them to get out of debt and to buy materials to carry on the work. Miss Broadbent then read the balance sheet which showed that the receipts came to £B6 2s. 101. leaving a balance in hand of £3 16s. 11d. That, slid Miss Broadbent was not as satisfactory as it sounded. Since drawing the report up, she had spent the balance in materials and there was still a bill of £.7 to be paid for rug wool. This year, they would not have a sal3 at. Mrs. Frost's to help them, and it was necessary to their very existence to make a larger sum that day than they had ever made at the annual sales. (Applause.) Mrs. FAIRCLOCOR said that as the oldest member— , with the exception of Mrs. Clay she was the only original member—of the Ladies' Visiting Committee, she could bear testimony to the efficacy of the Brabazon employment scheme. When it was first brought forward, she confessed she was rather doubtful' of the result. The material the ladies had to work upon seemed so hope- less. The work was intended only for those in the hospital who could do nothing else, and the inmates seemed so apathetic and indifferent that she really thought they never would sew or knit, or do anything of the kind. Mrs. Edelsten and Miss Broadbent, with their energy and perseverance, seemed to do wonders and she was sure many people would be quite amazed 'at the quantity of work which was brought forward at the annual sales. She hoped Miss Broadbent would be able to report a substantial credit balance as the result of the sale. (Applause.) Mr. FORSILAW, as vice-chairman of the House Com- mittee, moved a vote of thanks to Mrs. Fairclough and said it was the Guardians' endeavour to brighten the lives of aged and respectable poor who had to be attended to in the Workhouse Hospital. Mr. HICKMAN seconded and the motion was heartily agreed to. Miss Broadbent's services were also acknowledged and the sale commenced.

div.head: AN EXCURSION INTO THE OCCULT.
div.p: AN EXCURSION INTO THE OCCULT.
Interesting Paper at the Academy.

This was the title of a lecture given by the Rev. C. Harvey Cook, at a meeting of the Warrington Society on Thursday evening. Mr. C. Madeley presided over a fair attendance. Mr. Cook said heaccepted with a certain amount of mental reservation the phenomena of occultism as a science of that which is hidden. He thought it capable of co-ordination with all our other knowledge, and did not believe it was so transcendent a.s common, not unintelligible but sensible. Palmistry was not a fraud. It was when palmistry descends to minute details as to the colour of hair, a woman's future husband that palmistry became a humbug. All parts of us were indications of us, and it only required a keen wit, and a retentive memory and an ability for deducting results from physiological conditions to fit one to undersmnd how true it was that men c treed their indications in their parts. Telepathy, which had been described as an alleged phenomenon of feelings and impressions between persons at some distance without any agency other than that of mind" was not a fallacy. Thought transference was not an allegation,it was an established fact. Our noblest literature, especially the Bible and the classics and Shakesperian works were full of tele- pathy. Wireless telegraphy had done his mind yeoman service in the study of telepathy as an illustration of what he took to be a permanent factor in our mental ' condition. In wireless telegraphy it was all a matter of harmony—one instrument being in tune with another. That,he took it, was the law of common and uncommon 1 I property in thought. If he had a low level of ment- ality he would only respond to a low degree. Given a higher level of mentality the response would be greater, the ratio increasing as his mental capacity developed. To most of us telepathy is foolishness be- cause" we are out of it" because our telepathic instru- ment or organization is too crude,too clumsy to respond to the mental agitation going on around us. He had had many interesting experiments in quite elementary examples in telepathy. Clairvoyance was another indisputable quality of men's minds if the Bible stories were to be believed. There was another sphere of the occult, spiritualism, upon which his own mind was not satisfied, though he confessed that on its refined side spiritualism attracted him,while I its gross side repelled him. Spirit rapping, and table dancing disgusted his sense of propriety by their utterly nauseating unnaturalness. He had attended several seances but never saw anything which appealed to the deeper moral and spiritual instincts of his nature. He I was not holding a brief for the occult, he said in con- elusion, but like all serious students he sought to in- crease his knowledge. The lecture gave rise to considerhble and animated discussion, Mr. Cook's remarks being Somewhat severely I criticised. The gentlemen taking part in it were Messrs. L. Greening, A. J. Jolley, 0. Lofthouse, W. H. J. Jen- kins, P. R. Roberts, C. Madeley, Dr. Naden. and Alder- ' man Bennett. The discustion was not concluded, and I will probably be resumed at a later date.

WEEK ENDING MARCH 11th, 1905. During the week, the following births and deaths were registered:—Warrington Registration District births, 50, deaths, 24. The excess of births over deaths was 26. _

The birth-rate was equal to 37.5. The death-rate from all causes was equal to 18.0 per 1,000 against 15.1 the average of the previous 4 weeks and against 19'8 the corresponding period of last year. The death rate from the seven chief zymotic diseases was equal to -7 per 1,000, against -9 the average rate of the previous 4 weeks and against 5.3 the corresponding period of 1901. div.head: [By Godfrey Dean.]
div.p: [By Godfrey Dean.]
The Great Taboo.

To every rule (it is said) there is an exception. Aud it applies to women, but in a different way. To every lover she is the exception. Thus is the rule main- tained and the proverb perpetuated. Phyllis has discovered herself in a new light. Woman's personal charms have swayed more empires —laid prostrate more hearts—than ever intellect alone. But if a dainty head is a thoughtful one, too, innocent guile may provide piquancy for the beguilement of poor man. Phyllis was in a particularly interesting mood. She put a taboo on the word "love "—only fifteen minutes after my call—in fact, I was not to talk about it. I was disposed to object,bnt exacted a bribe instead. "Every Christian name has a meaning," I said, with seeming irrelevance. "And mine ?" she asked, unguardedly. "Yours is Phyllis, of course ; the meaning is—not allowed." She quite failed to look displeased. "This is very unconventional, you know," I said, referring to her great taboo. "Have you ever before done anything unconven- tional ?" "Is it impossible," I said, " you can ever think so badly of me as that? I mean, that you could not imagine me ever doing anything unconventional ?" "Is it," demurely, "a bad opinion, then ? " " It should offend a man of character." "What other unconventional thing have you done ? " she asked. "In what way? As a lover, or--" Otherwise "Phyllis said, hurriedly. I reflected. " I have smoked a cigar with a band on." " What a crime ! " " Not altogether, for I W 39 not found out. Besides, I took it off before it burnt ! "
" And what °wait, have yea to on: ?'—with pre- tended severity. _ .

Being tempted, of Collfs3, I eil. " You 533 I was in 10--" She gave ma a reproachful look. • "--I ought to say, I knew you then, Phyllis. It is the same thing." " You remember our arrangement ?" she pleaded. " That we were not to talk of—Phyllis ! Or was it, say —Phyllis !" " 'rat you were not to talk about "--she hesitated —" love." Phyllis blushed ; Love blushed. " I have not mentioned love,yet it was rather selfish to reserve to yourself the right to speak of it," "Oh !"—ffith a delightful access of colour, " how can you!"

"I am sorry," I said. " I don't believe you are," Phyllis replied. This was true. I was still a Pagan, impenitent. " I will promise not even to suggest the word," I said, " if you will be perfectly frank with me on one point." "Men are always making conditions," she said. Some men even in love, I thought. A.nd woman, the superior sex, gives herself unreservedly ! "What is yours ? " Phyllis said. "It is asking much, I al mit ; the subject itself is one from which a man might reasonably be warned off." "Do tell me," she urged. So I burned my boats. "Can a man be sure—or practically so—before propasing whether or no he will be accepted?" • "Why should you be interested in that question?" she said, quickly. Which was nice of Phyllis. Then I think she realised the inference that might be drawn from her remark, and turned her face away, apparently regret. ting her impulsiveness. After a brief silence, " Of course," I suggested, " I have no pers3nAl retsJa. My attitude is one of entire detachment. There is no necessity for me to ask the question. May I say that ?" She smiled, which I accepted as " Yes." " But I would like to know." She hesitated, while I, not to embarrass her, looked interestedly out of the window. " Yes, or I should think," Phyllis said, blushing furiously, " a man could nearly always make some- what certain."

"But." still refraining from looking at her, " you do not say how the man is.to find out first if he will be accepted." . " Why," Phyllis said, with a little more animation, "he must consider what she thinks of him and how long she has known him, though that does not always matter." " Of course not." "And finally, and most important of all, he must choose the moment. If she likes hint, all other things being well, the chance nearly always comes to the man when his suit will be successful. He must take the opportunity." "I see. Ho must seize the psychological moment?" Yee " Why, presuming she is nnt yat; say, quite in love with him, sheul&this particular moment Decor, as you suggest, at some time or other ? " " Because there is some quality in hint which she likes. She probably will be unaware of the reason, and the man more particularly." " That's hardly promising for the mom, is it ? " " Why," said Phyllis, laughing now, "how stupid you are." " Please explain." "The man must find out what her likes and dislikes are. He must learn--" Her voice had sunk lower and lowar, and new she stopped. " Oh, this is absurd of me," she exclaimed. "It isn't," I declared, firmly. " Play fair, or I revoke." She put up her hand. " Shut your oyes, then." " What else ?" I said. She resumed in a low tone. "He must learn what trait of his appeals to her, if only occasionally." " And then ? " " He must make the most of it—that of course delicately—for the time will COM 9 when her nature will be responsive to influence from him." " Yes ? " " That is all." I opened my eyes. "You would make a charming professor," I said. " Why ?" " You explain things so well. But I should only think of one professorship for you." Phyllis did not understand. " A professorship of 10--" You must not say it," sloe said. Then, as a compromise, " hit you may whisper

Lymni Ratepayers'Association Formed. On Tuesday evening a meeting was held at the Plough Hotel Lyn= at which it was decided to form a Ratepayers' Association, "The object of which is to watch the proceedings of those local bodies which have the power to spend money raised by the rates and generally to take such measures as may be deemed advisable for the protection of the ratepayers of Lymm district." In moving the formation of the Association Mr. G. P. Dewhurst remarked that money was spent a little more freely than if the spending of it was under the direct influence of the ratepayers.—Mr. W. P. Rylands said there was nothing in the proposal to form that association which was in the least degree antagonistic to the District Council.—Mr. Dewhurs. was elected president of the Association, Mr. W. Gould hon. sec., Mr. A. Pollitt hon treas., and Messrs. A. Watkin. A. W. Callender. W. P. Rylands, T. A. Flampson, A. B. Boumphrey, J. Palmer, C. J. Miller, J. E. G. Groves, J. Coxon, J. Newmarch, W. P. Mackendrick, and W. Bayley, vice-presidents.

div.head: PASSIVE RESISTANCE.
div.p: PASSIVE RESISTANCE.
THE REV. H. DUNNICO'S REASONS FOR RESISTING.

Preaching at the Parr Hall on Sunday evening the Rev. H. Dunnico took for his subject "Religion and the !Education Act; or why I break the law." His remarks were based on the text We ought to obey God rather than man," and were addressed to a large congregation. He wished it to be distinctly understood he said, that he had consented to speak upon that subject under a strong sensejof public duty. He had no love for strife for strife's sake, but he spoke under pressure of what he believed to be a Christian duty, and would endeavour to say nothing inconsistent with the motive which impelled him. When great truths and great principles were at stake the man who held those truths and pro- fessed those principles and was silent upon them betrayed his trust, outraged his conscience' and violated and degraded his manhood. For over three years he had lived amongst them, and he had had the honour of preaching week by week to the largest and most representative congregation of Warrington's public life in the town. Hence they were perfectly justified in asking, as some of his friends had asked, "How is it that you, a Christian minister, you who have preached to us the duty of obedience to law, are summoned to appear in the dock of a police court, to be punished for resist- ing the law?" They had a perfect right to ask that question, and he, as their minister, was bound to answer it. He had always had great faith in the fairness of the congregations that gathered there week by week. The voice of the people was not always the voice of God, neither was the verdict of the crowd always just, but if he had to come up for judgment before any tribunal he would rather stand before a body of people such as he saw before him than before one of those cliques of 1 men and women to be found in Christian churches, and all other organizations who believed that to thorn and to them alone had God given right to pronounce judg- ment. Mr. Minnie° repudiated the idea that if it had not been for the Anglican Church the children of the poor would have remained uneducated. The Anglican Church had opposed education as long as she possibly I could, and when she did take up the work it was in a I spirit of jealousy and primarily in the interests of the Church itself. It was due to the efforts of Noncon- formists that elementary education was established in this land, and that it was not only untrue but unjust to I say that we were indebted to the Anglican Church for such. He wished to be studiously fair to all. He was no bigot, hence he felt justified in making it clear that the Anglican Church was not entitled to the claim she so frequently put forth. Under the new Education Act there were no longer voluntary contributions or voluntary schools. The schools were State schools, and the right of the clergy or the denomination to manage their own schools had gone with the voluntary element in their support. He opposed this Act because it viola- ted a fundamental principle of English constitutional law in allowing public money to be spent upon that over which there was no adequate public control and because it inflicted a great unjustice upon a body of men who deserved their respect, and who ought to be allowed to pursue their careers in accordance with that merit, namely, the teachers who had been trained for the purpose of educating the children in voluntary day schools. At the present time nearly 1,800 head teacher- ships were closed to all who refused to subscribe to the Anglican or Catholic Creeds, although the whole of the salaries for those positions came out of the State funds and the teaching profession was just as much a branch of the Civil Service as the Customs House or the Post Office. He also opposed the Act because of the injus- tice it inflicted up )n the parent and the child. In oon- elusion -Mr. Minnie() said he made no apology for doing what he did. The greatest men of history were all law-breakers, Bunyan, Hampden, Thoreau and every noble martyr. He had put his hand to the plough and he should not look back now. The battle had com- menced. They had not sought it, but it would go on and never end until they had gained religious equalit y in the sight of the law for all men and for all churches and until every child in their schools and every teacher in his professeon was as free from the fatal interference of the priest and parson as the wave upon the sea or the wind upon the mountain. MORE CASES AT WARRINGTON.

Warringtons passive resisters, seven in numbers made their appearance in the police court on Nlonday,"to show cause why they should not pay the balance of the poor rate still owing by them." They were the Rev. W. J. Roberts,3o,Parker street, Gs. 11d. •, Emma J. Fieldhouse, Bridge street, 10s. Bd. ; Evan E. Hughes, 10, Crosfleld street, 7s. 6d. ; Thomas Dale, Priestley street, is. 4d. ; Edward Howard, 192, Padgate-lane, ss. ; William Clatworthy, 21,Lovely-lane,6s. Bd. ; and William G ilop, 69, Buttermarket street, 10s. Dr. Fos was the presiding magistrate the other magistrates present being Alderman Hutchinson and Bennett. and Mr. C. Jackson Holmes. Mr. W. H. Woodcock, assistant overseer, conducted the cases the proceedings being of a very formal character. All the defendants, with the exception of Mr. Howard were present, but only one ventured any remonstrance, the Rev. W. Roberts saying he declined to pay the ;rate because he had more respect far what was right and just. The Bench made an order upon each of the defendants, and said the amounts would be placed on bile warrant for those defendants who appeared. A lamina' position has arisen in the case of the Rev. J, F. Matthews: minister at the Latchford Baptist Chapel. Determined not to pay the education rate he made over his goods to his wife. The overseers sought to make Mrs. Matthews responsible for the rate and served the demand note upon her.Mr.Matthews protested against this course and his name was subsequently put in the demand note. On Monday he paid the rate less the amount for educational purposes, and it now remains to be seen what steps the overseers will take to recover the balance. Mr. Matthews some time ago announced his intention of going to gaol in preference to paying the rate and the situation is therefore an interesting i one.

div.head: CASES AT DARESBURY. FOUR STOCKTON HEATH RESISTERS SUMMONED.
div.p: CASES AT DARESBURY. FOUR STOCKTON HEATH RESISTERS SUMMONED.

Four passive resisters from Stockton Heath wore on Tuesday summoned before the magistrates at Daresbury. IThey were NIT% 11. Law, Whitefield-road, the Rev. J. S. 'Hughes, Bedford-street, the Rev. H. Dunnico, Fairfield- road, and Mr. E. Lloyd Jones, Ellesmere-road. The 1 respective amounts owing were, ss. 9d., 45., 55., and ss. 3d. and in each c :se tho magistrates, Messrs. 3. E. Parr (chairman), J. White, W. Long and H. Nield granted an order for recovery. Mr. Law : lam present not because I object to the 1 payment of the poor rate—that I contended I have paid —but because I object to pay. Mr. E. A. White, who acted as magistrate's clerk in the absence of Hr. Henry Greenall : The magistrates have decided that they will only hear you on legal ques- tions. We know what you are going to say. Mr. Law: lam summoned to show cause why I should not pay the rate. I think in all courtesy that a few moments might be allowed. The Chairman : The law is the law, and we are here to administer it. and to listen to any objection to the legal part of the question. As to any reasons that may enst in your own mind, lam afraid we are not here to go into that. Mr. Law: But we cannot urge any legal objection to the law, and we have to abide by it. The Clerk : That is all we can listen to. Do you ask for one ,oarrant for the four?

-- Mr. Law: Yes, I think so. The Clerk : It saves a little expense, and that course is adopted throughout the country. The Rev. J. S. Hughes : I think it is scarcely fair that we should be asked by the summons to show cause why we will not pay, and have no opportunity in court of stating our case. The Clerk : You can show any legal reason, but not a moral reason. .

Rev. J. S. Hughes: I beg your pardon. That is not stated. The Clerk: The magistrates have r.ded they will only hear legal objections, and if you are not satisfied it is open to you to take any course you like. Rev. J. S. Hughes: And the magistrates have raled before listening to the case. The Clerk: Only legal objections will be heard. If you can show that the rate has not been properly laid, or that it has not been demanded, it is open to you to do so. Rev. J. S. Hughes: But that is as unjust as the law itself in regard to the education question. 'You don:t listen to what I have to say. I may have a legal objection. The Clerk: If you have a legal objection, make it. Rev. J. S. Hughes: Then, first of all, 11 state that this' (the summons) is wrong. I know you regard it as a quibble, but why cannot a court of justice issue a cor- rect summons ? 'lbis is not correct. It states that I have not paid the poor rate. When the summonses are issued it would not be too much trouble to correct the matter, and strike out the wrong words. I appeal to the magistrates. Why should a court of justice issue a wrong summons ? The Clerk: It is part of the poor rate. Rev. J. S. Hughes: It is perfectly true, but I have not refused to pay the poor rate. I have not hesitated about that; it Is simply this addition to the Education Act that we refuse to pay for. We protest against the injustice of the Act in thia way. We don't want to waste the Court at all,

..... The Clerk : Very well, then. Rev. J. S. Hughes: I suggest that those words should be omitted in the next summons. The Clerk: I am afraid we are not prepared to listen to your suggestion. The usual order was made in each case, only one warrant, however, for the four defendants to be issued.

Sudden Death. Mr. H. Parker (60), 79, Pierpoint-street, was found dead in bed yesterday morning by his wife. He had been suffering for some time from bronchitis. He went to work as usual on Thursday and when he retired to bed at night he was apparently in his usual health.

div.head: COMPULSORY MILITARY SERVICE.
div.p: COMPULSORY MILITARY SERVICE.
RESOLUTION IN SUPPORT AT THE SOCIAL SERVICE LEAGUE MEETING.
"That the principles and proposals of the National Service League are worthy of the support of this meeting." . .

By a'Majority of 19 votes the above resolution was carried at the weekly debate in connection with the Social Service League held in Golborne-street schools on Thursday evening. The proceedings were of special interest as Mr. Shee, M.A., secretary of t!fle National Service League, attended to expound the arguments in support of compulsory military training and to move the resolution. Mr. J. A. J. Morton presided and the attendance included Captain G. R. Crosfield, Lieutenant Broadbent and the Misses Broadbent.

In the course of an interesting and able address, Mr. Shee said the real aim of the National Service League was the preservation of peace and the physical,ma.terial, and moral improvement of the people. He contended it was an absolutely logical course that if we were to maintain peace—considering the fact that mankind is what it is, with many evil passions, and that nations were only enlarged editions of the individual man—we must make it worth while for everybody to keep peace, land make it disastrous and lamentable for him to go to 1 war. That was the essence of the policy of the true lovers of peace who belonged to the league. He be- lieved that if we extended to all men the responsibility for the maintenance of peace, and let them understand that if there was war they would be called upon to fight and not to send some poor fellow men, often from the lower section of the community, to do the fighting for them, there would be an enormous incentive to the maintenance ot peace. The country at the present time, he contended, was not prepared for war. It was true that the navy was in a most satisfactory condition, and that thanks to the brilliant administration of that splendid sailor and businessman, Sir John Fisher, the navy was in a more efficient state than it had ever been in since the days of Nelson. With regard to the army, if the expenditure were any criterion, we ought to have the most excellentarmy in the world for it was the most extravagantly costly. Last year the British Army alone cost 06,000,000, or £163 per man. That gave a nominal force of 270,000 men, but there were practically only 192,000 men available as home and colonial troops. Of that number 46,000 -were officially declared to be non- effective. The militia were 35,000 short of the estab- lishment voted by Parliament, and the volunteers were also many thousands below the standard. It war not, however, merely a question of numbers. We could do with a very much smaller army if we had a more effec- tive one with better physique, better morale and altogether better material. The physique of the British soldier had been lowered steadily year by year for the last fifty years, and at the present., the standard was 21 inches below the heightand 151bs below the weight of the average British boy of seventeen. The death-rate in the British army was three times as high as in the German army, and the disease rate was three and a half times as high. When they considered that in 1900 we enlisted a considerable number of British soldiers who were under 7 stone 21b, he thought they would realize that the voluntary system was per- haps not quite such a magnificient thing as some of them would fondly believe it was. When we were at war with the smallest white power on the face of the globe the strain placed on the reserves of the British army was so enormous that it was almost at breaking point. The League did not pro- pose to touch the voluntary system as applied to the regular army, but that system, if it was to do its work thoroughly, must be founded upon a national scheme of training. We must not go into the gutters and slums of our cities to find the defenders of the empire. They should be men who had been trained in a national citizens' force and who, not for fear of the I workhouse or starvation but because they chose that 'career, entered the army, with a good prospect before them. Dealing with the auxiliary forces, Mr. Shea con- tended that the volunteers were unable to give sufficient time and attention to their duties to prepare themselves adequately for the tremendous business of war. It was not the fault of the volunteers ; it was the fault of the 1 system by which we attempted to thrust on these I patriotic men the business of national defence which could only be adequately fulfilled if shared by all. The league proposed, in the first place, that every child attending school should receive a sound physical training and be instructed in the duties of citizenship and patriotism. To continue the system every able-bodied youth ought to go through a short course of military and naval training to prepare him to take his place efficiently in the day of need. They did not propose conscription—that a man should be taken away from civil life for several years and put in barracks. Mr. IShee detailed the Swiss system of train- ing on which the proposals of the Leagne are founded and contended that if all the men of England had to perform the common duty of citizen- ship side by side, it would soon be dstermined that slums should be swept away. The question, he believed, was one with which the future of the nation really lay. (Applause). Mr. J. ELWELL, junr., seconded the resolution. Mr. TRoWE was the first speaker to voice the opposi- tion. He contended it was unnecessary to have an army for home defence. Ever since he was a boy the .bogey of a foreign invasion had frequently been raised, but there were no signs of the invasion being attempted. If national service would do much to bring about peace, how was it that it had not prevented the war between Russia and:Japan? When men were kept in a state of preparedness for war their passions were soon aroused and they were ready for anythine. He would ask the meeting to bear in mind that in the House of Commons on Wednesday evening. Mr. Balfour made the statement that in the opinion of the Imperial Defence Committee invasion for the purpose of conquest of these islands was an impossibility. Mr. HITCHEN also opposed the motion and contended that the army was not short of men. More inducement should, however, be offered to men to take up the military profession and thorough competence on the part of the officers should be insisted upon. Mr. GEORGE DALE strongly supported the motion and condemned the indifference which many displayed on the subject. Mr. E. WYNNE JONES said he hated all war because he did not believe any grievance would justify the killing of man by man. Tae voluntary system ha,l not, he contended, been properly tried and tested. Considering the vast expenditure on the Army and Navy, it was a standing disgrace if we were not erepared for war. If greater facilities were aiven for men to rise in the Army there would be no lack of proper recruits. He was not at all in favour of the military aspect of the works of the league, but if it could do anything for the physical training of the children and the demolition of slums he would be in hearty co-operation with that branch of their scheme. He would fight against com- pulsory military training because it would trench upon liberty. The auxiliary forces could, in his view, be made a greater power if they had more liberty to work out their particular plans without so much interference from headquarters. Captain CROSFIELD considered it very foolish for the Primo Minister to have made such a statement as to the alleged impossibility of invasion, because other nations would simply laugh at us. All military history taught that defeat entered through the gate which was con- sidered impregnable. We had to face the possibility that for a certain period an enemy might be able to establis local supremacy at sea and pour troops into this coun- try. It would be nothing short of murder to pit volunteer battalions, unaided by regulars, against thoroughly trained troops like those of Russia and Japan. He felt vary strongly the injustice of our volunteer system. Why, he asked, should the Volunteers alone do what was every man's duty? Mr. HAWTFIORNE and Mr. ELWELL supported the motion. The latter speaker said he believed it was absolutely necessary that every Briton should do his level best to put his country in a state of efficiency to meet any contingency which might arise. Miss M. S. BROADBENT spoke in support of the motion. Though she felt that there were worse things than war, she held we ought to do all we possibly could to ensure peace. No country, in her opinion, would be as likely to attack us, if it knew we had an enormous reserve of trained men. We were less likely to enter into unnecessary war if we felt the whole country would be affected. Then again, the physical deterioration in England was lamentable and we ought to be only too glad to seize the opportunity offered by the I.anue to try and improve that state of affairs. Mr. EFIEE briefly replied to the points raised and sub- /flitted that the adoption by every modern, up-to-date civilised nation of the principle of universal service during the past thirty or forty years, was the root of the progress of the principle of arbitration. On a vote being taken the resolution was carried by 20 votes to 10.

PA-11-LSI( COUNCIL 11IFETING.—The proceeding of the Council opened with a special meeting when Mr. A. L. Kaye was elected to 511 the place of Mr. F. R. Roberts. The ordinary council meeting then took place and the overseers accounts were read to the members, showing a balance in hand of £l4O. Small items of expenditure were also passed. The general meeting next followed. The chief subject discussed was the question of rates. Here, as elsewhere, rates show an upward tendency. A resolution was passed protesting against the increase and asking the County Council to exercise care in their expenditures in order to keep down the rates. Several other items were mentioned and the meeting terminated after a vote of thanks to the chairman, Mr. J. Charlton Parr.

Councillors Boyle and Wainwright and Mr. M'Elroy (Tramways Manager) were present on Wednesday at a meeting in London in opposition to the railway com- panies, proposal to run motor 'buses in Manchester and elsewhere. On terms that haveheen suggested the tram- way companies will be prepared to withdraw their opposition to the railways. The answer of the railways will be reported to a meeting in London on Monday.

,r DEATH OF MR. JOHN DIGNUM.

I Another Warrington worthy passed away on Saturday evening in the person of Mr. John Dignum, Dunelm, Great Sankey a gentleman who earned the sincere res- pect of all with whom he came into contact during the course of a long lifetime. Mr. Dignum, who -,as in his 83rd year was for upwards 0f..10 years in the service of Messrs. J. Blundell and Son (now the Pemberton Colliery Company Ltd.,) and by his uprightness of character and conscientious attention to his duties he earned the confidence of his employers who rapidly promoted him to a position of trust. He took a deep interest in religious life and for over twenty years was a deacon at Wycliffe Congregational Church, acting also as secretary to the church, and secretary to the deacons. He for a large number of years conducted a young men's class at the ‘Vycliffe Sunday School being one of the most competent teachers ever connected with the school. He had a large acquaintance with theology and he was an unusually apt Greek Testament scholar. In fact there were few men so well versed in theological matters which he made a special study throughout his life. He severed his connection with Wycliffe in 1893 when he divided his attendance be- tween St. Mary's Church, Sankey, and the Sankey Wesleyan Church. In politics he was . a Liberal-Unionist though he never took any active part in party affairs. For a number of years he was. a member of the Board of Guardians being regular in attendance at the meetings of that authority, and dis- playing a considerable knowledge of the poor law. Latterly he became a member of the Penketh Parish Council, being connected with that body for several years. He leaves a large family of sons and daughters and an extensive circle of friends to mourn his loss One of his sons is a Congregational Missionary in India

div.head: CRICKET SEASON.
div.p: THE CRICKET SEASON.
Warrington Club to Join a League.
GREATER ENTHUSIASM NEEDED.

Cricket enthusiasts are already looking forward to the commencement of the 1905 season, and the Warrington club having joined a League there should be an increase of interest in the doings of our local wielders of the willow. The members of the Club assembled at the Patten Arms Hotel on Monday evening for their annual meeting and having reviewed the past season's work, proceeded with the election of officers and other business. Mr. Fred Howard, the president, occupied the chair and there was a good attendance.

div.head: -FINANCIAL.
div.p: -FINANCIAL.

Mr. R. H. SILCOCK, hon. treasurer, presented the accounts, which showed a favourable balance on the year's working of £3 17s. 7d., an adverse balance being reduced to £69 15s. id. Taking it altogether, Mr. Si'cock added, the Club had had a very good year. The weather during the summer was very good, but the attendance of members was not up to the average. There seemed to be a lack of interest and enthusiasm which had often characterised the members in preced- ing years. What the reason was he did, not know except that there might be other attractionS! He hoped for better results this year. They had joined a Cricket League and expected to get increased gates and better matches. Mr. Silcock appealed to the members to take a greater interest in the Club. If each member could bring forward a new member their funds would be increased a hundred per cent. (Hear. hear). The CHAIRMAN proposed the adoption of the balance sheet. He said he quite agreed with the treasurer that they had really had a very fair season. They had a small balance in hand on the year's working whereas in other years they had had a deficit. He was sorry to say they had a number of resignations. One serious competitor was the Golf Club at Appleton, but he hoped that those members of the Cricket and Bowling Club who had joined that Club would not altogether forget them and would get down to Arpley occasionally. (Hear, hear.) Mr. R. T. FA TRCLOUGH seconded the motion, and said he was pleased to find the balance sheet was a better one than he had dared to expect. He hoped that next year they would be able to wipe off more of the deficit. (Hear, hear.) The motion was passed. THE PRESIDENCY. _ _

Mr. 11. T. FAIRCDOUGH said he was sorry the Presi- dent had not be able to see his wly to accept office for another year, but the Committee had succeeded in gett- ing a gentleman for the office who would give satisfac- tion to everyone. He proposed that Mr. William Gill be president. (Applause.) Mr. H. H. SILCOCK seconded, and said Mr. Howard had been an ideal president, and they were all sorry they had failed to induce him to continue in office for another year. But in Mr. Gill they were hoping they would have a suitable president. He had been identified with the Club for a long time and had always given it his support. With Mr. Gill as president he thought they might look forward to a successful year. rho motion was carried with acclamation. MR. HOWARD'S SERVICES. Mr. 301 IN DEWHIMST moved that Mr. Howard be elected a vice-president. He said he attributed the favourable balance sheet in some degree to the interest Mr. Howard had taken in the affairs of the Club during his presidency. He had often been present, and by his citeerful disposition, joviality and friendliness did a great deal towards keeping the Club together at a rather critical time. . .

Mr. C. H. HNSWORTII seconded, and said no one knew better than he the help and assistance Mr. Howard had been, not only to himself but to the Committee. The motion was carried with applause. Mr. HOWARD, in reply, said it had been a matter of great pleasure and delight to him to do what he could for the Club, and he had been amply repaid by the kind- and courtesy shown him by the members of the and, in fact, all the members of the Club. OFFICERS.

election of officers was then proceeded with Mr. R. H. Silcock was re-elected hon. treaittrer, with Mr. R. H. Daintith as assistant treasurer Mr. C. H. Unsworth, hon. secretary; Mr. E. A. Connor, captain, and Mr. Callan, deputy-captain of the let eleven ; Mr. E. Pierpoint. captain of the 2nd eleven: Mr. W. H. Podmore, match secretary, Mr. T. Cooper, bowling secretary ; Mr. R. N. Silcock, secretary to the tennis section ; and Mr. D. Tinning, auditor. The committee was elected as follows :—Cricket section : Messrs. J. W. Bibby, P. B. Hawtin, E. Connor and E. Pierpoint ; bowling, Messrs. R. H. Daintitb,ll.ll. Evans,S. Pearson and H. Ferguson; tennis representative, Mr. J. B. Isaac.

Mr. NNSWORTH, upon being re-elected secretary, said it was now thirteen years since he was appointed Isecretary of the Club. He had always taken a great interest in the Club and was very fond of it. Although , he played golf he shoul4 aever give up the Warrington ' Cricket Club—(hear' hear)--and he hoped that a good many others who had joined the golf club would be animated by! the same spirit. (Applause.) During the I thirteen years he had been secretary he thought some I substantial progress had been made. Notwithstanding the apparent decrease in the number of members, he had not the slightest fear but what the Club would I always go on in a satisfactory manner. At the present time he believed it was one firmer foundation than ever before, and he did not see the slightest reason why it should not become more and more prosperous. Their assets were larger, while their liabilities were very ; small. Their debt, was £6O, but he remembered the time ;when it was over £2OO. Mr. Henry Fairclongh said they never prospered except when they were in debt— (langhter)—and he thought there was some truth in the suggestion. Although they had a smaller membership, a nesbtoh should dldrougns. H a(waeya scr: ihtheart.)he idea that they were go one to ; APPLICATIONS FOR SUB LETTING OF GROUND. The SECRETARY reported the receipt of a letter from the Police Athletic Club asking permission to use the cricket and bowling grounds on certain days and offer- ing to pay £l2 for the season. The Rev. E. J. Will- cocks, headmaster of the Grammar School, had written asking if the boys might be allowed tn play their cricket and football matches on the club's ground, at a. rental of £2O. Considerable discussion followed, the general opinion being against the application of the Police Athletic Club, and in fa:mar of that of the Grammar School with certain restrictions. It was pointed out that the Grammar School might become the means of providing new players for the club. The matter was referred to- the committee for final decision. On the motion of Mr. T. COOPER, seconded by Mr. :I. DawittrnsT, a cordial vote of thanks was passed to Mr. Howard for presiding.

Progressive Labour League. The weekly meeting of this leaaue was held at the Liberal club on Tuesday evening, Mr. T. Barnes pre- siding over a good attendance. A paper on " The unemployed question " was submitted by Mr. J. H. Morton who said that the drink evil was one of the principal causes of the distress which prevailed. div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
CRiELTY TO CHILDREN!

At the Warrin-gToc;-P-olicae-COUW,On-M.onday, Patrick Burk, 28, Fennel-street, was charged with ill-treating his children by causing them to be exposed.—Mr. Browne, who prosecuted on behalf of the N.S.P.C.C., said the defendant had been drinking heavily. On the 3rd March he went home drunk, and his conduct was so bad that his wife went to Inspector Cox, of the N.S.P.C.C. The Inspector, together with P.C. Baxen- dale, went to the defendant's house and found him acting in a mannenalmost beyond description. The children were terrified and had run out of the house. Burk was quietened,but as soon as the officers left he continued his conduct and his wife and children were so terrified that they went to sleep at the house of a relative. Since Christmas his conduct had been such that his wife on a number of occasions has had to take the children out of the house at midnight to go and sleep elsewhere. Defendant promised to reform and upon that under- taking the case was adjourned for three months.—A police charge against Burk of being drunk and disorderly was adjourned sine die. TIMFT FROM TIIE CO-OPERATIVE STORES. Robert Weigh (16), 165, Wellfleld-street, and Henry Page (16), 44 Mill-lane, were charged with stealing from the Co-operative Stores, Lovely-lane, some time between 1.15 on Tuesday and 7.30 on 'Wednesday morn- ing, £2 es. 6d. in cash, and a quantity of sweets and tobacco.—Superintendent Monaghan stated that the Co•operative Stores were left safe on Tuesday. On Wednesday morning it was found that the premises had been entered through the cellar grid, and the articles mentioned in the charge stolen. Detectives Meacock and Clough made enquiries, and found that the prisoners had been changing copper for silver. It also transpired that Weigh had given his mother 10s., saying he had won it in a football sweep, while the other lad gave his sister 13s. When arrested the prisoners had 28s. in their possession.—Mrs. Weigh said she could not do any good with her son, who had gone worse since his father died. She would like him to be sent away.—The magistrates recorded a conviction against the lads, and allowed them to go with a warning. COWARDLY ASSAULT.—John Henry Rowe, Bewsey road, was charged with assaulting Mary Ellen Whitney, Hanover street, on September 16th. Mr. Unsworth who conducted the case for Mr. T. S. Steel said that a summons was issued against the prisoner, and as he did not appear in answer to it a warrant was issued. On the date in question, Mrs. Whitney having received a complaint from her daughter as to the prisoner having used abusive language, she went to the house of a Mrs. Clare, with whom Rowe lodged to speak to him. Rowe was upstairs and on coming down immediately rushed at Mrs. Whitney and violently assaulted her. Mrs. Clare interfered and was bathing the complainant's face which was bleeding, when the prisoner again rushed at Mrs. Whitney and again assaulted her. Prisoner who pleaded guilty, was sent to gaol for two months with hard labour.

FOOTBALL IN THE STREET.—For playing football in the street Thomas Williams, 28, Robson-street, Mozart Wilcocks, 103, Manchester-road, and George Morris, 10, Ifelsby-street, were each fined 2s. Gd. CRUELTY TO A HORSE.—Thomas L. Law, 179, Win- wick-road, was lined in the costs (Gs.), for illtreating a horse by working it in an unfit condition. The evidence of Inspector Gibson of the R.S.P.C.A., showed that the horse was suffering from stavin and was totally unfit or work.

div.head: Warrington P.S.A. Society.
div.p: Warrington P.S.A. Society.

An open meeting was held in the Co-operative Hall Sankey-street, on Sunday, and was largely attended. The chair was occupied by Mr. R. Pearce Williams. The Apollo Quartette gave the two selection," Remem- ber me," and "Rock of ages," and Miss Miller was heard to advantage in the solo " Entreat me not to leave thee." Mr. B. Wadsworth was the accompanist. The Rev. C. Harvey Cook addressed the meeting, his subject being, "As in a looking glass." He dealt chiefly with Warrington and its surroundings, and wondered if all the people took the interest in the town they ought to do, and whether they attempted to make it better. He sometimes thought that people forgot the good of the community and thought only about themselves. The welfare of fellow creatures was part of the Christians' duty, and he hoped that besides reading their Bible from beginning to end they would extend their thoughts to those around them.

div.head: WARRINGTON & KNUTE:RD
div.p: WARRINGTON & KNUTE:RD
BIG LIGHT RAILWAY SCHEME WITHDRAWN.
Strong Opposition at the Inquiry at Warrington.

So strong was the opposition manifested at an inquiry conducted at the Warrington Town Hall on Tuesday by the Light Railway Commissioners into the applica- tion of the Cheshire Light Railways Ltd. to construct a light railway from Warrington to Knutsford that, after a long hearing, the promoters withdrew the scheme. Great interest centred in the proceeedings and there was quite an imposing array of legal gentle- men. The Commissioners were represented by the Hon. A. E. Gathorne-Hardy, Colonel G. F. 0. Boughey, R.E., C. 5.1., and Mr. Henry Allen Steward. They were accompanied by the Secretary to the Commis- Somers) Mr. Allan D. Erkine). Mr. q. J. Talbot, barrister, appeared on behalf of the promoters of the scheme and local authorities' and other parties interested were represented as follows : Mr. Sam Moss, M.P., for the County Council; Mr. G. Rhodes, for the Bucklow Rural District Council, and the Parish Councils of Mere, Tabley, and High Legh ; Mr. Boyd Merryman, for the Urban District Council of Knutsford ; Mr. F. E Smith, for Lord Egerton and Lady Leighton Warren; Mr. Trevor Lloyd, for Colonel Cornwall Legh, Mr. Egerton Leigh, and Colonel Lang- ford Brooke; Mr. Clode, for the Cheshire Lines Com- mittee ; Mr. Walter B. Dendy, for Mr. W. C. Dunkerley ; Mr. George F. Ashton, for the Rural District Council of Runcora ; Mr. Caldecutt, for Cannn Dean; Mr. J. Lyon Whittle, for the Warrington Corporation; Messrs. Robert Davies and Company, for the Thelwall Pai ish Council and Mr. J. St. Vigor Fox; Mr. Colin Maclver, agent for Mr. J. St. Vigor Fox, Mr. W. Andrew Jones, for Mrs. Ann Gregson ; and Mr. Josiah Longland for Mr. G. Hankey.

div.head: -SCHEME DETAILED.
div.p: THE -SCHEME DETAILED.

In outlining the scheme Mr. Talbot, on behalf of the promoters, pointed out that Warrington was a very important town, with a population of 70,000 and was surrounded by a very populous neighbourhood. It occupied an important geographical position because at Warrington there was the first road bridge over the river after leaving its mouth. That, he believed, was the only important road-bridge for a considerable dis- tance to connect Lancashire and Cheshire and conse- quently it carried a very heavy traffic. The proposed railway would run to the bridge crossing the Ship Canal at Latchford, and at the north side of that bridge the Warrington Corporation tramway system terminated. The Corporation had, however, power to cross the bridge to the terminus of the proposed light railway. The Corporation tramways also extended to Stockton Heath and the Corporation had powers under the Light Railway Act to run from Stockton Heath to Latchford._ South-West Lancashire was at present

INTERSECTED BY A GRRA.T SYSTEM of tramways and light railways—he believed something like NO miles of them were already in operation. The South Lancashire system at present ended at Ashton-in- Makerfleld, about five miles from Warrington, but the company had power to extend the line to Warrington. Therefore any Cheshire light railway which connected with the Warrington system, would before the lapse of any considerable period, be in connection with the great South Lancashire tramway system. \ Varrington was also in the important position of being on the Man- chester Ship Canal and on or very close to the Bridge- water Canal and it had an excellent railway communica- tion with London, Liverpool and Manchester. Any connection with Warrington must therefore establish a connection with a much greater area as well. The proposed length of the railway was ten miles. Between Warrington and Knutsford the railway communication at present was of the most defective kind, the.distance covered being slightly over thirty miles, and involving a seventy minutes journey. With very few exceptions it was always necessary to change, and the only route passengers could take to avoid changing was via North- wich. Probably it was partly due to the awkward rail- way service that Knutsford was not a very large town, and did not appear to be at present very rapidly growing. He did not think he need seriously argue from a business and tangible point of view that Knutsford and the district between Knutsford and War- rington must,beneflt by the construction of the railway. It must be to the advantage of the farmers in that agri- cultural district to be brought into communication with the markets of Warrington and the places with which Warrington was connected, and he need not remind the Commissioners that the primary object for which the Light Railway Act was passed was that agricultural dis- tricts should be opened up and given facilities for con- veying produce to the market and obtaining require- ments from great industrial and manufacturing centres. , There was A CONSIDERABLE EXCURSION TRAFFIC to Knutsford in the summer, the town being attractive and picturesque and the road along which the railway would be constructed carried a great number of visitors by means of brakes, &c., during the summer time. Then again, it was obviously an advantage to Warrington business people to be able to have as wide a choice as possible of outside neighbourhoods in which they could live. The light railway would provide facilities for the benefit of business and professional people in War- rington who wished to journey to and from the town each day. There were still four tanneries on the route I but he understood two others were given up as, largely owing to the lack of means of transit, the firms found it impossible to carry on business profitably. Another! advantage of the railway would be that it would furnish facilities to the corn millers of Warrington for the collection of grain and dispatch of flour. There was, he would also point out, a very considerable out- put of lime, particularly at the well-known soap and chemical works of Messrs. Crostleld and Son and he understood that the firm sent out a much less quantity of lime to the district between Warrington and Knuth- ford in proportion to other districts' simply for the reason that there was less facility for conveying it there. If the light railway were sanctioned, it I would obviously facilitate communication with Manchester from all the districts that lay between linutsford and Warrington. Altogether the district seemed to be " cut out "for a light railway, in fact it was,he should think,the very case contemplated by Parliament in which a light railway would be of advan- tage. Counsel pointed out that some years ago, before the Light Railway Act was sanctioned, powers were obtained to construct an ordinary railway line between Warrington and Knutsford in connection with the Lancashire, Derbyshire, and East Coast Railway ; but the Scheme so far salt affected the Warrington district was not carried out. The light railway, it was proposed, Iwould be laid mainly in the centre of the road, but for a short length—mostly in the more urban parts—it was I proposed to lay it on the waste land or grass at the I side of the road. Clause 12 of the Order provided that where the metalled portion of any road on which the railway was laid was of less width than 27 feet the cora- pany:should widen;i r. so that it should reach that measure- ment, and the width of the footpaths was to be preserved I as it was on the first of November of last year. There was a proviso that if it was impossible at any time to widen the road to that extent without clearing or removing buildings the company should obtain a cer- tificate to that effect from the road authority. At Knutsford there would be a loop to connect the railway I with the Cheshire Lines Committee's goods station. Mr. Clode (who represented the C.L.C.) pointed out that the committee could not consent to compulsory , powers for the light railway to run into their goods yard, under any circumstances whatever. I Mr. Talbot said he saw no reason why a settlement I should not be arrived at. He thought he was right in saying that throughout the whole of the route there was no point, with one exception, at which anything in the nature of an engineering difficulty arose. The place in question—where the Bridgwater Canal crossed the road at Grappenhall by means of an aqueduct— could, lie believed, be dealt with perfectly well by sub- mitting the mode of working to the regulation of the Board of Trade. The cars would be so constructed that they could be opened and shut at will. No passengers would ride on the top and the total height would be about It feet. The lowest part of the bridge in question was just under 14 feet. The promoters had bean in communication with the Board of Trade and their belief was that they would not come into conflict with any Board of Trade regulation in regard to the matter. Near the aqueduct a road from the direction of Lymm joined the main road and it was almost certain

ESTIMATED COST ef the system worked out at about £5,140 per mile, and he thought the Commissioners would come to the con- clusion that that was a careful and economical estimate, that no money had been wasted, but that the railway had been designed on such lines that it ought to be a commercial success. With regard to the local autho- rities affectO, there was considerable difference of opinion. He observed it had been stated that the scheme was not supported by any local authority, but that was very far from the fact. It was opposed by several authorities -he hoped in many instances on points of detail which could be very easily adjusted, but it might be that some Councils, for some reason or other, were altogether opposed to the scheme. The promoters had the important support of the Warrington Corporation. With regard to he Run- corn Rural District Council, he hoped to be able to tell the Commissioners that they did not oppose the scheme. Mr. G. F. Ashton: The Council do oppose it in its present form. There is one deviation they asked for Subject to that, they will withdraw their opposition and it will then depend upon the County Council. Mr. Talbot continuing, said the Parish Council of Latchford and Grappenhall supported the scheme, and the Parish Council of Thelwall and Urban Council of Lymro did not oppose it. He was sorry to say the pro- moters had not been able to come to an agreement with the Knutsford Urban Council. One of the objections urged by that authority was that the undertaking would injuriously affect the natural scenery of the neighbour- hood. The promoters, he would point out, had made various suggestions, which they thought were not un- palatable to the Council, with a view to min- mising, as far as they could, any interfer- ence with the amenities of Knutsford. Tha promoters were willing and anxious to do that. The Bucklow Rural District Council had raised several objections—such, for instance as that the railway would be dangerous to the public using the road, which would apply to any light railway scheme anywhere. The Parish Councils of High Legh, Tabley, and Mere were also opposed to the undertaking but he thought the commissioners would see pretty clearly that the parishes which were small rural neighbourhoods were those in which land owners had very considerable influence, and that might have something to do with the attitude adopted. Dealing with the opposition of the Cheshire County Council, Mr. Talbot pointed out that the views of that authority on light railways had already been very carefully con- sidered by the Light Railway Commissioners. In the application for the Warrington and Northwich order, which was officially confirmed rather less than two years ago, the County Council appeared and took a very great variety of objections, and also pursued their campaign before the Board of Trade. With one or two trifling exceptions, all their objections were rejected by the Board of Trade. The Council did not indicate in their objections the real nature of the points they wished to have met, and they had consequently sub- jected the promoters to g,reat inconvenience. The objections were for the Most part of a general character. The Council reserved the right at the inquiry to advance such further objections as they deemed advisable, and he contended it would have been fairer and more convenient, if the Council had forward- ed all their objections previously. Between Warrington and the Bridgewater Canal there was no opposition on the part of land owners. Mr. Longland : Yes. Mr. Hankey asks for a modifi- cation as to the width of the road and the provision of footpath. Mr. Talbot said there was a large estate company known as the Warrington Estates Company which sup- ported the promoters and Mr. William Lomas also supported. Lord Barrymore did not oppose, neither did Mr. Hill's trustees nor Mr. William Long. From High Leigh to Knutsford they were practically in the position that all the land owners objected to the scheme. The land o .vaers iii WI it district were comparatively few in number. They were gentlemen of very good position indeed and he would deal with their opposition with all respect. He thought that, speaking generally, the landowners in that neigh- bourhood opposed equally the proposal of the Lanca- shire, Derbyshire and East Coast Railway, without convincing Parliament that they:were right and thatithe promoters of the undertaking were wrong. Mr. F. E. Smith : That proposal was only opposed by Lord Egerton on points of detail and he had no diffi- culty in arranging terms. His opposition to this is of a totally different character. Mr. Talbot said the real point the landowners had in view was the desire to preserve a certain SECLUDED OR SPECIALLY ATTRACTIVE CHARACTER. to their own estates and the neighbourhood of Knuts- ford. When they got land in the neighbourhood of great industrial and manufacturing districts, it was not possible to maintain wholly the rural districts untouched by the turmoil of manufacturing centres. In other words, it was not possible to exclude the inhabitants of manufacturing districts from the rural neighbour- hoods. Such objections as had been urged would militate against improved means of communication anywhere. There was, he admitted, very considerable opposition in point of numbers and importance from the landowners at the Knutsford end, and it was for the Commissioners to judge whether they ought to weigh seriously against the public convenience which the railway must afford. It would probably be urged by their opponents that the promoters would be able to call comparatively few witnesses from the Knutsford district and few farmers who farmed land there and who certainly, one would have anticipated, would derive benefit from the construction of the railway. He con- tended that a knowledge of the conditions of the country which the line would serve at once showed the necessity for the improvement. The promoters had met all the reasonable requirements of the local authorities and they were hopeful that the evidence would be such as to obtain the sanction of the Commissioners to the scheme.

that the Board of Trade would require some special Yes, most of them for services rendered. precaution either in the way of slackening of speed, or The solicitor to the Company is the holder of 2O? signalling so that people using the side road Yes. would not be surprised by theapproach of the cars.
