Jr at all? That it is not a matter I can say definitely. It is proposed to get the order and get the capital from somewhere else, or some other company with capital to take it over from you. That may be the course; but I cannot be sure. Have you one single local authority in whose area the line is going to travel which is here to-day supporting you? I believe there are four. Which are they? Mr. Talbot : Warrington, Latchford, Grappenhall and Lymm. In Lymm the road goes over six furlongs, and that is a Cheshire County Council road. Mr. Scotter : Yes. Mr. Talbot explained that Lymm and Thelwall did not oppose the scheme, and Latchford and Grappenhall supported it. Mr. Hatton (solicitor) : I represent Thelwall and I do not oppose, subject to conditions. Mr. Moss (to Mr. Scotter) : You were the engineer of the Warrington and Northwich light railway. Mr. Scotter ? Yes. On that occasion you had the local authorities behind you, and had local people with capital backing you. Yes. Although you got that order in May 1903, have you cut a yard of turf yet or done anything in the nature of a railway? No. But we have made considerable progress towards that end. What progress have you made? In getting plans, which is a most important item. How many years have you got in which to construct the railway, according to the Order? I think it is four. What kind of traffic are you going to take? Are you expecting anything betides passenger traffic? Yes. We expect the goods traffic will gradually develop. Have you any local capitalists, farmers,or landowners who may bring produce and goods, supporting you? Yes. From the suburbs of Warrington? And from the Knutsford end as well, I believe. A GREAT PROPORTION OF CAPITAL PROMISED. Mr. Rhodes (representing the Bucklow Rural District Council): Northwich is a much larger town than Knutsford and has considerable industries. Yes. You don't suggest there are industries at Knutsford? I know there are not. Although you have had the order two years, have you obtained any capital at all? lam not prepared to say that. It is a confidential matter. I can only say emphatically that a great pro- portion of the capital is promised. Subject to certain ' electrical arrangements we shall be in a position to commence to construct in a short time. Is a good deal of that capital promised by the con- tractor ? ot a penny of it. Have you taken out any figures with regard to what you expect to be the receipts on the Warrington and Knutsford railway ? Considering the population at either end and along the route,and the success of the Warrington tramways,l think they will come up to the average rate of traffic which the various light railways already constructedare carrying. That is a very nice long speech, but very vague. I want figures. Have you reckoned what your receipts would be on this line for passengers and for goods? Yes, I have reckoned them. Will you give the figures? No. I haven't got them with me. At the Warrington end of the line, you are looking to your income from passengers who will use the railway as an extension of the Warrington tramways? Partly. But there will be a through traffic to Knots- ford as well as the goods traffic. You don't look for any picking up of passengers on the way between Grappenhall and Knutsford ? Yes, we do. There is a population in between of some thousands. Have you formed an estimate as to what traffic you will pick up on the roqd between Grappenhall and Knutsford, and what your receipts from it will be ? No I cannot say I have taken that by itself. A good deal of the traffic will be through from one end to the other. Further questioned, Mr. Scotter said he had obtained evidence from the district to the effect that 40,000 people visited Knutsford annualy, exclusive of the great numbers who went there for the May day procession alone. With regard to the supply of electricity the promoters proposed to take over the Knutsford Light- ing Order and erect a station, if necessary, at Knutsford. As an alternative, he had a scheme before him to supply the power from the large station at Northwich. Mr. Moss: Supposing you get the whole 40,000 to visit Knutsford by travelling on the light railway from Grappenhall at a return fare of Is. 6d. what would the income be? Mr. Scotter: From that particular item in the revenue we should make £3,000. From Grappenhall to Knutsford is a purely agricul- tural district. lam putting it to you that the whole traffic into Knutsford, if it came on the line, would not give you more than your working expenses. That particular traffic from that particular district. You are taking away all the other largest paying traffic and you are supposing that no more than 40,000 would pass along the line during the year. I suggest that what is really wanted is an extension of the Warrington tramways to Grappenhall and that might pay. Without that, there is nothing else. I Certainly not. Is not the Warrington Estate Company supporting you in the scheme? Yes.
Their land is in the neighbourhood of Latchford.

Are they not supporting you or the purpose of develop- ing their estate as a suburban part of Warrington? That among other things, certainly. Further cross-examined, Mr. Scotter said there would be trailers behind the cars for the purpose of carrying goods. Mr. Rhodes remarked that one of his contentions was that the laying of the tramway at the side of the road in certain parts would materially affect the rateable value of his district. KNIITSFORD OBJECTIONS.

Mr. Scotter was also cross-examined at considerable length by Mr. Boyd Merriman, on behalf of Knutsford Urban Council,with regard to alleged dangerous points. Mr. Merriman asked if the overhead wires at Knots- ford would not be a grave disfigurement. Mr. Scotter said he would be very glad to get rid of them, and he had suggested the adoption of the surface- contact system in Knutsford. Mr. Talbot said he thought the promoters would be prepared to meet the Council on that matter. RUNCORN DISTRICT COUNCIL SATISFIED. In answer to Mr. G. F. Ashton, Mr. Scotter said it was the intention of the promoters to make the devia- tion at Latchford from the original plan. Mr. Ashton ' expressed himself satisfied with the proposed alteration. In answer to a landowner, Mr. Scotter said every cit./ cumstance in connection with the road would be taken into account before settling the speed. Generally the idea was to run a half-hour railway service each way. Mr. Scotter was also questioned by Mr. Hatton (Messrs. Robert Davies aid Company), who represented Mr. J. St. Vogor Fox. Answering Mr. Trevor Lloyd, (who appeared on behalf of Colonel Cornwall Legh and others), Mr. Scotter said everyone who lived between Warrington and Knutsford would benefit by the scheme. The promoters relied principally on passenger traffic, although they had a ' reasonable'expectation of getting goods. Mr. Trevor Lloyd : Is there any place on the route where you are more than 3.1; miles from a railway station? Mr. Scotter : That is a new idea. (Laughter.) Rather an awkward one. (Renewed laughter.) No, it is not. Is this not a nice little scheme by the Warrington Estate Company to develop their land ? Certainly not.

div.head: MR. SCOTTER CALLED.
div.p: MR. SCOTTER CALLED.

1 Mr. R. H. Scotter, engineer of the scheme gave evi- dence in support of the application and said the distance I between Latchford and Enntsford was ten miles. He I described the various railway means of communication I with Knutsford which, he said, involved a thirty miles . journey occupying about seventy minutes. By the light I railway he believed the journey would be accomplished t in about half an hour, although the speed would largely I depend upon the Board of Trade regulations. The gauge I proposed was the same as had been sanctioned for the i Warrington and Northwich railway and the Warrington I Corporation tramways. The car proposed to be used lavas only eleven feet high and had been used successfully in many towns in England and on the continent. At the i outset the company:expected to rely to a great extent on I passenger traffic. As the scheme developed he believed there would be an opening for a considerable goods traffic which would greatly increase until it became a very important factor in the receipts. The total esti- mated cost of the permanent way was £63,p00 which,of course, was exclusive of electrical equipment. The gradient of the road approaching the aqueduct at Grappenhall was 1 in 38 on one side and 1 in 28 on the other. The difficulty to be encountered there was the narrowness of the aqueduct which could not be altered without a considerable amount of trouble to the Canal Company. Caution would have to be exercised, but he believed the public would be sufficiently safeguarded by the Board of Trade regulations. He had ascertained that 2,168 vehicles passed into Warrington from Cheshire weekly by means of the Latchford Canal Bridge. The pedestrian traffic between Warrington and Latchford was estimated at 61,000 a week. Cross-examined by Mr. Moss, witness said he was un- able to find an instance of 'tarred macadam having been used in the construction of a light railway approaching a town of 70,000 inhabitants, as it was proposed to be used in this case. With regard to the Grappenhall aqueduct, it was only safe for one vehicle to be under the bridge at a time. The width of the road there, apart from the footpaths, was 15 feet. As to safeguard- ing the public, he thought there could be an arrange- ment to isolate the portion of the railway approaching the aqueduct and make a regulation that no car should proceed on that isolated portion unless there was a clear run through. A system of signalling to warn users of the road that a car was approaching could be adopted.

div.head: FINANCIAL ASPECT.
div.p: THE FINANCIAL ASPECT.

Mr. Moss: Who are the promoters of tins scheme? • Mr. Scotter : Tho Cheshire Light Railways Limited. What is the share capital of the company? I am not quite sure. I think it is £1,500. May I suggest that Mr. Seater is the, largest shareholder? Yes. You have 513 shares, I think, out of the 1,016 allotted ?

div.head: ORIGIN OF THE SCHEME.
div.p: THE ORIGIN OF THE SCHEME.

Mr. Smith, --;;i:;o aipea-red-fOi:LOr-ci-ig;e;ton and Lady Leighton Warren : lam suggesting this scheme does not spring from genuine popular local demand but from your head, and the heads of gentlemen who are fond of speculation. Mr. Scotter : Unfortunately every piece of private enterprise that is•not backed by the money of the County Council or the Corporation has got to have a certain amount of speculation. And is this a scheme which possesses a great deal of that ? I don't say it contains any more than any other scheme. , The fact is that the whole idea of the railway is yours at Westminster, and not the farmers along the road?

- Certainly not. For several years the matter has been discussed between various people that I have spoken to Between whom ? Several people. Mr. Henry Greenall and Mr. Hall ? Yes. And the other members of the Warrington Estate Company. Aro their others who have discussed the scheme ? No. Do you know that five of the directors of the War- rington Property Association are allotces in the light railway ? I do not.

div.head: CAPITAL.
div.p: THE CAPITAL.

Further questioned by 1`..1r. Smith, Mr. Scotter said £lOO,OOO was the capital, with power to borrow an additional £33,000, There would be a station at the commencement of the line, one at the Dog and Dart, one in the district of Lymm, and others as they could arrange with the local authorities, and, of course, one at the terminus. They would bare to agree to buy the land wherever it was agreed upon. The stations were for the convenience of the public and they could pick up passengers as was done on tramways.

Mr. Smith : My contention is that the public don't want the railway. Mr. Scotter : That is a matter of opinion. Further interrogated, Mr. Scotter said that if they could get anything like the average amount of traffic now obtained by the various light railways the scheme would more than pay. He could not give the slightest idea of the proportion for goods traffic and the propor- tion for passenger traffic. As he had said before, the goods traffic was a thing that had to be made in Eng- land so far as light railways were concerned. He denied that the surface-contact system was a failure. It was being used successfully on the Continent, and that was the place where they often had to go for their experi- ments.

It was stated at this point that the Cheshire Lines Railway had agreed to withdraw their opposition on condition that the branch railway into their line at Knutsford Station was made by agreement and not by powers conferred. in answer to a gentleman representing a property owner in Knutsford, Mr. Scotter said there was some- thing in common between Knutsford and Warrington which were separated by ten miles of space. There was a wish on the part of a great many people in Warring- ton to go to Knutsford, and many people from Knuts- ford wished to go to Warrington. The names would be given when the evidence was called. If they carried goods there was a suggestion that the Cheshire Lines should give them facilities for entering their yard. They would not carry goods unless they had facilities to do so.
Mr. Stewart (one of the commissioners) : Unless you have an agreement with the Warrington Corporation you cannot carry goods into Warrington? Mr, Scotter : That is so.
And unless you have ;1;-a.reement with the Cheshire Lines Committee you will not carry goods into Knutsford ? No.

By Mr. Talbot : He saw no reason why Knutsford should not benefit by dealing with Warrington. This was an ordinary mercantile promotion, and he made no secret about it. The public would also benefit if the schemes were carried out. He was not justified in mentioning names, but he confidently expected that the financing of both this Order and the Northwich Order would be arranged within a short time. Mr. T. Longdin, borough surveyor of Warrington,said he considered it would be a benefit to the district to get a connection with Warrington. Mr. John Fairclough, an ex-Mayor of Warrington, and a partner in the firm of Messrs. J. Fairclough and Sons, corn millers, said his firm did a fair amount of business between Knutsford and Warrington. He thought the construction of the railway would enable the firm to extend their business in Cheshire. THE SCHEME WITHDRAWN.

At this stage the inquiry came to an unexpected termination, the promotors withdrawing the scheme. Mr. Talbot said they felt the difficulty they were in owing to the unreasonable and shortsighed attitude of the local authorities, and they did not propose to continue with the application. The Chairman : You have made a gallant fight.

It might be taken as a sign of the times that the medical mission was being taken up with such interest, and he hoped that the noble efforts which were being put forth in that direc- tion in the East would be eminently successful, and that the work would be blessed. (Applause.) The Rev. W. R. COLE, secretary of the medical mission auxiliary of the North of England, appeal for an increased interest in the object of the meeting. div.head: MEDICAL MISSIONS.
div.p: MEDICAL MISSIONS.
Sleeping Sickness Described.
MEETING AT THE PARR HALL.

The great value of medical missions is indisputable, and it was with an object of creating an interest in the welfare of such organizations that a meeting was held in the Parr Hall on Monday evening. At this gathering which was under the auspices of the Medical Mission Auxiliary of the Church Missionary Society, the Right Rev. the Lord Bishop of Liverpool presided over a large attendance being supported amongst others by the Ven. Archdeacon Madden, Dr. J. H. Cook (medical missionary in Uganda), the Revs. Canon Willis, E. C. E. Carleton, Morley Stevenson, W. Bracecamp, J. Davies, B. Percival, W. Pollock Hill, and A. Inglis. Medical missions, said the CHAIRMAN, formed the most striking development in modern missionary work. We had our evangelical missions for teaching the Gospel, our educational missions for instructing the children, and our literary missions for supplying Christian literature to the more intellectual members of heathen communities. But greater than all these, he ventured to think,was the medical mission, and he only wondered that we had not such missions long ago. (Applause.) Experience had shown us that when a knowledge of medicine was combined with a love of God the mission became a wonderful and real power, as a tremendous hold was given to the man who displayed kindness and medical skill. (Hear, hear.) Where had the triumph of the Gospel been greater than in , Uganda? Although not yet 30 years old the medical mission had made its mark and the people of Uganda were sending out their own missionaries to neighbour- ing tribes and winning them to Christ, and it was' amongst that noble and loveable race that Dr. Cook lived and worked. (Applause.) Dr. Cook and his brothers were distinguished members of the University of Cambridge. Both as men of science had got careers before them, but they put them on one side, preferring to go out as medical missioners amongst the heathen. Both had already enriched science by their researches in Central Africa, but they had done much more by planting the Cross of Christ deeply and firmly in that wonderful land. (Applause). Dr. COOK said the object of medical missions was primarily spiritual, but that object couldnot be attained unless the medical work was as efficient as it could be made, and if the missions were worked merely to be held out as a bait to get the natives to come and hear the gospel, they were dishonest. (Hear, hear.) In the hospitals on the mission field they had opportunities for study as unique or even greater than in England and if some of the specialists only knew the character of the cases which medical missioners were called upon to treat, sheer professional jealousy would compel them to go to the mission field. We in England could hardly realize the physical distress which existed in heathen countries. He was assured when he went to Central Africa that there was no sick- ness amongst the natives. He might as well have been told that people did not die in Africa. When he went into the homes of the people in Africa he saw sickness and distress in forms which appealed at once to his heart. Sleeping sickness alone, although it only made its appearance four years ago, had caused the death of 100,000, natives. That mortality was truly appalling but that was probably not the real number as the natives calculated it as being three or four times as great. The disease was confined to a strip of land ten miles wide, runaing round the shores of the Victoria Nyanza. The disease, which was spread by the tsetse fly was unsparingly fatal and he did not think there was a single instance of a patient having recovered from the disease. It was being studied by experts, who, it was to be hoped,would find a remedy for it. (Hear, hear),lt was generally supposed that sleeping sickness did not cause istress but the reversewas the case. The people were slow to complain, but h 3 had had complaints from largo numbers of the pain arising in the early stages of sleep- lag siskness. The dissase was slowly spreading, and if it was not checked before it spread to other provinces the results would be awful to contemplate. Small-pox sometimes broke out amongst the natives in such violent epidemics that he had never seen similar cases in England. The medical missioners did not, however, fear that disease, as they had no conscientious objectors to vaccination, and as the result pf wholesale vaccina- tion the disease had been almost stamped out. Dr. Cook proceeded to detail thellarge amount of work the medical missioners in Uganda did, and said only men of the highest medical capacity and ability were needed for the work. Archdeacon MADDEN said he believed the only way we could reach Mohammedans was by means of medical missions. He was looking not only for a revival in England with regard to personal religion, but one that would lift us out of our selfish Christianity and help us to realize the great mission, "All the world for our

div.head: MOTOR NOTES.
div.p: MOTOR NOTES.

The truth of the aphorism that " a little learning is a dangerous thing" is never more clearly demonstrated than when we peruse advice upon motoring topics which has evidently been penned by one just emerging from his own novitiate. Some hints upon buying a second- hand car appear in the pages of a weekly contemporary, and, save for the fact that there may be those who will trust implicitly to the advice tendered and suffer accord- ingly, they are almost ludicrous to any motorist having even a fair knowledge of the points of a petrol motor. For instance, the prospective buyer of a second-hand vehicle is implored to make sure, first of all, that the compression is good. "If otherwise, a part of the explosive force will be wasted, with the naturally result- ing loss of power." The writer evidently knows nothing of low compression engines, and would doubtless con- demn a 9-11 h.p. Clement—to quote only one instance —as utterly useless. This particular type has very little compression indeed ; but there are few cars Of similar h.p. that can hold her when she is in good running order.

Having satisfied himself with'iregard to the compres- sion, the buyer is then directed to have the engine started," and carefully listen for any knocking sounds, which would indicate wear in the bearings of the piston- rods." Not necessarily would they do so, for knocking in the engine may be due to many causes, ranging from a too advanced ignition to wear on the big end bearing. The condition of the gears, the propeller shaft and the wheel are next passed in review, and, provided these are satisfactory, the motorist is then advised to take an "exhaustive trial run " and clinch the bargain.

It will be noticed that nothing has been said concern- ing the possibility of a leaking pump, of faulty water or lubricating pipes, of a worn clutch leather or brake lining, of dilapidated steering gear—of indeed, the hundred and one trifles that, nevertheless, must all receive attention before any sensible man will take over a second-hand car in exchange for hard cash. There are a good many things that may be wrong even if there is plenty of compression and no knocking in the engine, and the buyer who will be content with the superficial examination laid down for his guidance is probably going to3learn in a very hard school much concerning breakdowns and wayside repairs to a petrol motor.

Another great point to be ascertained—which our motor noter appears to have disregarded entirely—is the date of the car in question. There are many excel- lent second-hand vehicles on the market, in good con- dition and splendid running order, which are not to be advised as purchases, save at very low prices and for use in a purely experimental manner. The reason of this is that they are out-of-date, and, therefore, their market value has elready greatly depreciated. When the new owners wish to get rid of them this will be even more the case, so that the money spent upon them will be practically thrown away, except so far as they have been useful as object lessons.

Quite recently, we ourselves were offered a 3-h.p. Benz for £l2—which is merely the price one would pay for an ordinary pedal cycle; but the type is thoroughly old-fashioned, and, therefore, unless a man is found who i is willing to gain experience with t., even the .Sl2 Benz will not be easy to dispose of ln the second-hand market. Of course, there is always the chance that it may be seen by some of these who have learned wisdom —of a kind—from the scribe we have been quotirg, in r which case it will doubtless be readily snapped no, for athsehceoimnspirsetssstihoenyims must be, parallel with each t, and even the wheels are, other when running.

The fact of the matter is that many persons who can steer a car and mend a puncture, more or less success- fully, exist under a misguided impression that they are, in consequence, full-fledged motor experts, and the result of this sanguine belief is apt to prove a little disastrous to their friends as well as to themselves. There is not an unlimited number of practical experts in the country, and of these the majority, at least, re- quire a rather high fee for advising upon the purchase of a car. When the great object is to keep down ex- penses to the uttermost farthing the prospective pur- chaser is thus either thrown upon his own resources or compelled to be guided by one who has,perhaps,as little really practical knowledge as the gentlemen whose advice we have commented upon here. We are not quite certain whether the Motor Car Co. (1905) Limited ex- tend their new (and very unique) system to the field of the second-hand car ; if they do, the mirchaser may be quite sure that by applying to them he will not only get the best advice, perfectly gratis, but also the best possible car obtainable at the price he proposes to pay. If they do not, they could probably make some arrange- ments with a competent man to see and report upon proposed bargains for their clients' convenience. At any rate, it would be worth enquiring about. Once this ' course would cost nothing and would commit the enquirer to nothing, whereas the purchase of a car upon the lines suggested to him by the authority we have mentioned would undoubtedly land him in a quagmire I of trouble awl consequent emiense.

div.head: NORTHERN UNION.
div.p: THE NORTHERN UNION.
NORTHERN LEAGUE.
First Division.
RESULTS OF SATURDAY'S MATCHES.

G. T. P. G. T. P. Batley Bradford 1 6-20 Runcorn 0 0— 0 Broughton ft. 0 0— 0 Leeds Halifax Leigh Oldham.. ......... ... 0 1— 3 Hull 0 0— 0 Widnes 1 0— 2 Hunilet Warrington 2 0— 4 Hull K. Rovers 1 0— 2 Wakefield Trinity 3 5-21 St. Helens 0 0— 0 Warrington v. Hull Kingston Rovers.

The return match between these clubs was played at Warrington. in the presence of about 3,000 people. Neither side was at full strength, Warrington being without Fish and Harris, while the Rovers had sub- stitutes for Starks and West. A strong wind and a wet turf militated against good play. Teams: Warrington.—Hallam, back; Kenyon, Dickenson, Berry, and Brooks, three-quarter backs; Isherwood end Thomas. half backs; Preston, Shugars, Cook, Belton, Jolley, Naylor, Swift, and Harmer, forwards. Hull, Kingston Rovers.—Sinclair, back; Phipps Madley, Chambers, and Winpenny, three-quarter backs; Gordon and Barry, half backs; Kemp, Windle, Towns- ley, Ellis. Osborne, Mullineux, Taylor, and Stevenson, forwards. Referee, Mr. W, W. Taylor, Hunglet. Touch judges Messrs. W. Critchley, Widnes, and J. Elliott, Birkenhead. Owing to the strong wind twenties were agreed upon the Rovers having thp first spell with the wind. They however, made little headway against the defensive work of the home team. On one occasion they should have scored easily, for Gordon got clear away, and had only to pass to Phipps for a certain try, but he held the ball too long. There was no score when the teams ,changed ends' and Warrington soon forced the pace. Thomas and Isherwood at half back, however, were strange to one another, and the poor undeistandiug among the backs spoiled numerous chances. A break- away by Chambers looked dangerous till Kenyon sprinted up and kicked the ball in touch. Preston kicked a fine penalty goal, and at half-time Warrington led by two points to nil. On the resumption the. Rovers tried hard to get the lead, but shaped little better, and all they got was a goal placed by Gordon. The last "twenty" was com- menced with the teams on even terms. Warrington attacked persistently Isherwood missing a nice pass near the line,whileglerry was held outside. Only three minutes remained for play when Preston was called up for a long-range penalty kick, and the cheering was hearty when the famous forward gauged the wind to a nicety, and gave Warrington the victory by two goals (4 points), to one goal (2 points).

div.head: WIDNES v. HUNSLET.
div.p: WIDNES v. HUNSLET.

•-- - At Widnes, before 1.800 spectators, on a bad ground in a perfect gale. Hunslet were weakly repreaented behind the scrimmage, the Goldthorpe' being the most notable absentees. The interval arrived with a blank scoring sheet. After the change of ends it rapidly became apparent that the visitors were profiting by the advantage conferred by the gale. The home team never- theless proved capable of holding their own, and from a mark by Ike Taylor, Alf Taylor dropped an excellent goal. Hunslet, aroused by this reverse, made a spirited effort t. score, but without avail. For a considerable Period play ruled at mid-field, neither side being able to secure more than a momentary advantage. No further score resulted, and Widnes secured the verdict by the narrow margin of two points to nil. WAKEFIELD TRINITY v. ST. HELENS.

_ At Wakefield before a moderate attendance. There was a strong wind, and the ground was in a heavy COSl- dition. Although the Trinitarians had to play against a strong wind in the first half, they were repeatedly an the attack, and Measor placed two penalty goals, and Malkin and Crosland each scored a try, the score at half-time being ten points to nil in favour of Wakefield. 'tithe second half the Trinity backs indulged in pretty Passing. and Baker, the old Brighouse threequarter, ran in a splendid try. Another fine bout of passing ended in McPhail racing over, Messer landing a goal. Newbould afterwards got over, and this being all the scoring, Wakefield won by three goals, five tries (21 points) to St. Helens nil. BRADFORD v. RUNCORN.

At Bradford. The visitors were without Jolley, who had been taken ill on his way to Bradford, and during the greater portion of the second half they were with- out the assistance of Padbury, who had to retire hurt. The home team had the advantage of the wind in the first half, and were generally on the attack. The for- wards cot possession of the hall, and the halves and three-quarters made splendid use of the chances that went their way. Dechan scored three tries and Eagers one, and at half-time the score was :—Bradford, one goal trrtd four tries (14 points), to Runcorn nothing. The visitors were not so hard pressed throughout the second half, but they merely looked like scoring when they visited the home territory. They hada good chance from a penalty on one occasion, but Butterworth failed to lift the ball. Later Dechan scored again, but hurt himself in crossing the line, and retired. Before the interval Francis, who had taken his place, also added a trY, and the final was—Bradford, one goal and six tries (20 points), to Runcorn nothing.

div.head: PAVING OF PRIVATE STREETS -- -- Objections to the Corporation Apportionments.
div.p: PAVING OF PRIVATE STREETS -- -- Objections to the Corporation Apportionments.

The magistrates at the Warrington Police Court were on Thursday called upon to bear objections made by Mr. Speadelow and Mr. W. G. Ward, to the apportion- ments made by the Corporation with regard to the paving of a passage in the rear of Dickinson-street. Mr. Wilson explained that the total cost of paving the passage was £159 9s. 7d. Mr, Spendolow had a frontage on the street of 44 feet 6 inches and to him was apportioned £l9 165 11d, of the cost. Mr. Ward was apportioned to £2O Gs. 7d. The passage at one end was 26 feet wide and at the other end 25 feet wide, whereas the width required by the bye laws was 20 feet. It was on account of the width of the passage that the objections were made, as the objectors maintained they were called upon to pave only ten feet of the passage. The owner of the property on the other side of the street had not carried the yards to the full length with the result that the passage was wider than was required by the Corporation. The Cor- poration, however, took it as they found it and whether it was wider than was necessary or not,did not concern them. With a view to decreasing the cost of the paving the Corporation had widened the foot- paths on either side of the passage, with the result that the amount in dispute in each case was only about 325., although a great principle was involved. Mr. John Fairolough, chairman of the Magistrates : Suppose a street which has to be 40 feet wide is built on on one side and a builder when erecting property on the other side leaves a space of 40 feet, will the person who built the first lot of property have to pave 40 feet ?

Mr. Wilson : That is an extreme case. Very prob- ably the centre of the street would be left unpaved. Mr. Spendelow said that when the property was built it was stated in the lease that he would have to pave 10 feet of the back passage. He contended that Mr Appleton was responsible for the extra width of the street and should pay for the extra width. Mr. G. F. F. White (magistrate's clerk) : The paving mentioned in the agreement is for the protection of the landlord who would otherwise have to do the work. Mr. Fairclough said the magistrates sympathised with the objectors but as they felt that the property NA ould be enhanced by the extra width of the passage they dis- missed the objections.

div.head: DIAGRAM 71.
div.p: DIAGRAM 71.
A scicw cannon ,at the top of the table. -- h. spot. cue" ball behind the red and about 3 nches from the cushion. Object white about 1 nch from the cushion and 2 inches from the cue

For example, in Diagram 71 the stroke :o play is a screw-back cannon, but the strength if the stroke must be so regulated that the red, after rebounding from the baulk cushion, comes :1 rest somewhere near the top cushion, other- wise the resulting position will most likely be ,ad. In pla3 jug such a stroke there is always a tertain amount of latitude for good strength, for the stroke will be equally good whether the red ;top just a -little short of the top cushion or whether it rebound just a little after reaching ;he top Cushion. So long as the red comes to rest it the top of the table, position will almost always be left, for the red will generally be wol/ placed for a pot or an in-off, and in addition an easy cannon may also be on. Too slow a stroke sill, however, not bring the red far enough up, and too fast a stroke will send the red down the table again after rebounding from the top cushion; thus in either case the resulting posi- tion would be very uncertain, and more likely :han not nothing at all easy would be left to con- thine with. Of course, in playing such a stroke the strength of the table, must be taken into ron6ideraLiort for a stroke that would bring the,• red nicely back on a medium-pace table would leave the red short on a very slow table, and would bring it up with too much speed on a very fast table.

_ Viihen the cue ball is only six or eight inches from the object ball, as on diagram 71, it is not very difficult to regulate the strength of the .stroke to the speed of the 'table, for when 'a one ball is comparatively elose to an object ball a screw-back may be played without much strength as well as iith plenty of strength, but when the objc:ct ball happens to be some distance from th,.% cue ball, say 12 or 15 inches away, it is no easy matter to screw back the necessary distance without imparting a good deal of pace to the chject ball. Were the red three or four inches faither from the ene ball than shown on the diagram it would require a very good stroke in- deed to screw back or. to the white without without getting too much pace on to the red, especially on anything like a fast table. Players who are pretty good at screw-backs should prac- tice screwing ba.:..k with as little strength as pos- sible. The stroke shown on Diagram 71 will afford very good practice if the red ball be moved about an inch farther down the table each time the cannon has been made without the red ball more than reaching the top cushion.

In playing screw-back cannons such as the one shown on diagram 72, it is generally far bet- ter to play the stroke off the cushion with side, for the simple reason that this method of playing the cannon gives more latitude for error in aim than when playing to cannon directly on to the second object ball. When playing without side to screw back straight on to second object ball. the cue ball must either come back right on to the ball or else strike the cushion very close to the ball, otherwise the cannon will be missed, and in trying to get full on to the ball it is very easy to miss it on the far side (this would be to the left of the ball as the player stands at the table.) By playing the stroke off the cushion with sids, (right-hand side in the diagram) the cannon will he cot even should the cue ball strike the cushion some little distance from the ball, and as when playing the stroke in this manner aim has to be taken nearly full on to the object ball there can be no fear of missing the cannon through the cue ball passing the second object ball on the far side.

Many ordinary players when playing screw- back cannons like the one shown in Diagram 72 strike the cue ball on the side near the second object ball ikstead of on the other side. ,Played in this way-the cue ball should it strike the cushion at a right angle will rebound in a direc- tion .ziwas. from the second obiect ball,

div.head: Dan Leno at Warrington.
div.p: Dan Leno at Warrington.

Sir,—Hating seen your aunouncement in last Satur- day's" Eraminer " re Dan Lean. I beg to state that he never appeared in the Empire Theatre. He appeared here in Warrington about 20 or :2 years ago in the old wooden building which then used to stand in Sankey-st. When he was here he had a Clog-dancing competition in which several local men took part, including Arthur Casey, and Patsey Grey, the competition being won by Molest named and be was awarded a belt which Dan Leno had offered. Dan Leno also appeared in the Royal 'Corrt Theatre when it was the Public Hall. This is about 30 years ?“.•.0. He came then with his stepfather and mother. These are the only two occasions he has been in Warrington as far as I can recollect. Hoping this will meet with your ,correspondent's requir em eats. —Yours faithfully,
A PLAYGOER.

div.head: Bases of Free-Trade.
div.p: The Bases of Free-Trade.

- -- Sir,—Last week I spoke of the common fallacy that excess in the value of imports over exports is paid for in money, and showed why this could not be when viewed merely as an abstract question. But suppose the reasons I gave were inoperative and we paid for imports over exports in this manner. What would happen? Mc-law of supply and demand, which affects money quite as much as it affects any other commodity would operate. I said that only as much money was coined as was needed for the purposes of exchange, and this woald not anything like equal in value the excess in an any one year of the value of imports over exports, but suppose it only amounted to a few millions the payme.ut of these few millions would denude us of, or withdraw from our circulation, this amount. Money would thereby be so much scarcer, and its exchange value would r:se in proportion. That is to say, an articlo, say a coat, the tailor had been previously getting St--;. for would MCP only bring him in 18s. It would therefore ia,eiately flow back to restore the Rot uiute is another very common fallacy connected with Ath matter. The advocates of Import duties claim to be the only real Free Traders, and assert that we who are following Cobden are only one sided Free Traders, or Free Im- porters. They speak'contemptuously of Cobden's prin- ciples and declare them to be antiquated, no longer applicable, and unfair. This latter description pre- supposes something that Cobden never gave any warrant he contemplated, viz., that he advocated the , abolition of all import duties especially those upon food in order that other countries would be induced by our example to:abolish theirs. That he did believe that our action would be of such enormous benefit to us that other countries, from motives of self interest, would follow our lead. I will not deny, but there was nothing in his advocacy which showed that he had such an object in view. He might believe that such would be one of the results that would naturally follow, but his primary object was to benefit his countrymen. This , was true patriotism,and the sneers of present day would, I be Tariff Reformers, about his little Engandism, come with an exceedingly bad grace. What was the condition of this country at that time? Its area in proportion to its population was small, as it is only more so, to-day. It was insufficient to supply all our wants, but we were a manufacturing wmciiie as we are to-day. The fruits of our industry were as much wanted by the people of other countries, as the fruits of their industry were by ourselves. A free exchange would have given us comparative comfort but artificial obstacles were placed in the way, so that this 'free exchange could not exist, with the consequence that, not one third, but a much larger proportion of our people were starving. Food was dear, wages were low, and industries were languishing. Even the agricultural industry which was supposed to derive the greatest benefit from import duties, was in a most depressed .condition. So that not only were a great many people out of work, but even those who had work got very low -wages when compared with the average of to-day, and yet the principal articles of food were very dear. It was to remedy this state of things that Cobden devoted his life. He sought to accomplish this by striking off the fetters which bound our commerce, and give us that free exchange above alluded to. This was not approaching other nations "with bated breath and whispering humbleness," and saying in bondsmen's key, "We will take oft our import taxes in your interests from the goods you send us, but we hope you will do the same with the goods we send you." He consulted nobody's ' interests but our own. The 'floodgates of commerce were thrown open and food admitted free of duty to a starving people, and who shall say now that subsequent events did not prove the wisdom of the act. True, others were incidentally benefitted by it, because the exchange enormously increased. We bought more, and therefore we sold more. Distress was Featly decreased if not abolished. The languishing industries revived, the people were given employment, wages rose, and food became very mnah cheaper. Besides getting higher wages,and therefore more money, the purchasing power of this money was increased, and it was found that a very much greater portion of the wage fund after the demand upon it for the purchase of food had been met, was available for the purchase of other commodities, consequently home trade vastly improved. I think I have now laid the ghost of unfairness, by showing that we consulted only our own interest; but another question opens up here, as something else is pre-supposed which has absolutely no existence. Our friends say it is "unfair," which is another way ef saying that import duties are paid by the senders of the goods and that by abolishing them, we relieve them of this contribution. This is so glaring a fallacy, that it ought not to be necessary to say anything in disproof of it. When a manufacturer is asked to tender for any goods for a country where import duties are charged, he generally quotes a price free on board at the shipping port, or the port of entry. Take the first case, suppos- ing an order results. ' The importer pays the freightage from the country of origin and the import duty which the government from the other country charges. Now suppose the manufacturers price is £lO the freight 10 i.ond theimport duty 10s. Before the importer can supply to the consumer, he has to charge the manufacturer's price of £lO plus freight, plus import duty, which makes it £l3 to him, and the manufacturer may know nothing of these two last items, as they are not included in his price at all, but the consumer has to pay them all the same. If this is not sufficient proof, the Tariff Reformers have supplied something that is indubitable When an import tax is imposed on any article one of two things happens. Either the tax is absolutely prohibitive, in which case the government would get absolutely nothing, or it may leave sufficient margin, between the manufacturer's price, plus the freightage, plus the tax and the selling price, to make business possible, in which case the government would secure the amount of the tax. But what puzzles me, is that all governments don't make the foreigners pay for all the expenditure of the country, supposing their own con- tention that the sender pays the import taxes is correct. If the sender does pay the tax, why tax any goods as low as possible? Why not tax them as high as possible? Especially,why exempt any of the goods from taxation? Yet this is what the Tariff Reformers propose doing. Some propose a low tax of 2s. on corn. others ss. others 10s. If it makes no difference to the consumer, why hesitate? Why not make it 10s, at once, or more if possible? They could then enga,,be in any buccaneer- ing expedition they chose, withoutbeing worried about the provision of the means. But the Tariff Reformers do not only not propose this,but they exempt two im- portant articles of food altogether, namely maze and bacon. Surely this is a mistake for it flatly contradicts their assumption that import taxes are paid by the sender, and not by the consumer, and provides an argu- ment that is irrefutable by providing that after all, the consumer does pay the tax.—Yours faithfully, A. RATHBONE.

The Mount, Grappenhall. Councillor Stott and the Next Election. Sir,—With your kind permission I should like to have a few words on the above subject in answer to your correspondent who signs himself" Nunqualm." It gives me the impression tha", after all, the Liberal party of Warrington are not so confident of success at the next General Election as they would have us I believe, or why should they seem so concerned about Councillor Stott giving a helping hand to one of his own party in Mr. Seddon., Has not Mr. Stott a perfect right to help whom he likes? Surely we are not so prejudiced as to expect a man to go against his own feelings and wishes in supporting any movement with which his ideas do not concur. I have no doubt Mr. Stott and also the party to which he belongs will give their votes, but it has nothing to do with me or even " Nnnqualm " or anyone else as to whom they shall give them. "Nunqualm" seems to forget that the Labour Party is a distinct party of itself, and, if I mistake not, it has also come to stay. Now, why should Mr. Stott, who belongs to the Labour party, be expected to give his support to the Liberal cause any more than you would a Conservative, or vice-versa? Then again, "Nunqualm" says "It would be far more straightforward if he and his party were to put certain questions to the respective candidates and then work whole-heartedly for the one who was prepared to support the measure,s for the good of the community they represent." es 'Nunqualm" the Tories and Liberals alike are all wonderfully prepared to support almost anything before the election, but how far do they extend th‘t support when they are once in the i "House," especially so when there s an important division? They seem to think more about retaining • their seats in Parliament than of serving their con- stituents. Take last week's division forlinstance on Mr. Churchill's motion, did all the Unionist Free Traders vote for it? I am afraid not, or the Government must have been beaten, and so it has ever been, whenever they find themselves in a tight corner they follow the leader 4:aid go against their own consciences for the sake o

remaining in power. Now then *Nunqualm," we have had enough of this kind of legislation and it behoves every workingman to seek his own salvation and that lies in being directly represented in Parliament, hence the Labour Party, and through that party alone can he get a sound and beneficial legislation and he would find it more likely to act than all the promises that come from either Tory or Liberal. " Nunqualm's" reference to the fire business and the Captain of the Newton Division Fire Brigade I look upon as so much rot. Then he goes on to say," what would Mr. Seddon say if the Liberals refused their help to him in his tight at Newton." Well, " Nunqualm," what will the Liberals of Warrington say if some of the Tory majority of the last election vote Liberal ? If I think rightly, neither Mr. Seddon or any other Labour candidate desires men to vote against their own consciences, they would rather stand or fall by their party principles, and, as those principles become more known among the working classes, the 4.4 hour party is bound to increase in numbers and I venture to say " Nunqualm," that in a few years time it will be, not the question of who the Labour party shall support, but which party is prepared to throw in its lot with the I.L.P. Earlier in his letter he also refers to " what Councillor Stott would have to say if the Liberals and progressives refused to help him in his Wald at the coming November elections because he is a Socialist." "Nunqnalm" -lam afraid has not made a thorough study of socialism or the Labour movement or he would know that all progressive minds would vote for him without any assistance whatever, as the prin- ciples of the party to which he belongs contain the very essence of progress, and I repeat, as workingmen become more in touch with those principles on which the Labour movement is based, it will take more than either a Tory or a Liberal programme or promise to shake them off. In reference to what friend " Nanqualm " says of the Rev. H. Dunnico, if Mr. Dunnico is the man " Nun- qualm "makes him out to be, well, he is not in want of men like" Nunqualm " or anyone else to advertise him. His own " cleverness " and "earnestness" of which " Nunqualin "speaks will do all that for him. My ' Opinion of parsons in general is, that they can say a great deal and give their opinion for the betterment of the people,but it stops at that. Of course there are ex- ceptions but they are few, and maybe Mr. Dunnico is one of these. The embodiment of the whole Labour movement is to do what our ministers of the Gospel preach about, the uplifting of the poor to a better standard of living and so make their lives worth the living by a just and honest legislation. In my humble opinion, herein lies the true Christianity. You make the same mistake as many others have done and still do, that is, you condemn a movement, or treat it with distrust, because certain individuals professing it do not come up to your ideas or way of thinking. That is not fair; if a movement, or the principles upon which that movement stands are for the general welfare of the masses, why condemn it, even if there are one or two individuals you may know that do not live up to it? That does not say the whole] movement is bad. You will find men in any movement, either political or religious who do not live up to the principles they assume, but, as I say, we must not condemns movement on those lines or lam afraid we shall have no move- ment left. And I maintain friend " Nunqualm" that because one or two members of the I.L.P. have not quite suited you and Mr. Dunnico, you have no right to throw mud at the I.L.P. by saying, "he (Mr. Dunnico) is far too clever and earnest for them, and naturally, of course they are jealous—nothing more, nothing less." In conclusion, I should like to remind you "Nunqualm," that Mr. Stott stated also, "that Mr. Seddon would work for the workingmen of Warrington as well as in the Newton Division," should he be sent to Parliament, therefore I think that Mr. Stott is only doing his duty in helping Mr. Seddon and furthering the cause of labour of which he is a strong supporter. 'lithe Liberals of Warrington want to win,they will have to work and not get quibb- ling over these trivial matters, and win by their own efforts and then if they do win the victory will have all the more honour attached to it.—Yours &c.,
FAIRPLAY.

div.head: WARRINGTON EDUCATION COMMITTEE.
div.p: WARRINGTON EDUCATION COMMITTEE.
Business of the Next Meeting.
The last meeting for the year of the Warrington Edu- cation Committee will be held at the Town Hall on Monday evening when the following amongst other business will be considered.

FEES TO BE RETURNED. The managers of the St. Ann's National School wrote to the Finance committee intimating that for the future the fees of those children in Standards V., VI. and VII. who make full attendances will be returned. This action is with a view to meeting the excess of school fees to which attention has been drawn by tbe Board of Educa- tion. Subject to the approval of the Board of Educa- tion the arrangement was approved. GYMNASTIC INSTRUCTION, .

The report of lti;K:inc'Sub-Committee appointed to consider the physical instruction given to the children in the public elementary schools, having been submitted to the Finance Committee it was resolved that the physical exercises in the schools receive more serious attention than hitherto,and that the head teachers be recommended in drawing up their time-tables, to arrange for shorter and more frequent exercises to be given. It was also decided that the scholars in the mixed departments of the Warrington British and Trinity National schools and of the secondary School, use the gymnasium for instruction in physical exercises given by teachers of those schools.

PENNY SAVINGS BANKS. A circular letter, dated the Bth February, 1905, from the Board of Education—calling attention to the desir- ability of establishing Penny Savings Banks in connec- tion with the public elementary schools—was submitted at a meeting of the School Management Committee, and instructions were given for enquiries to be made as to the number of such Savings Banks at present in exist- ence in or associated with the schools in the Borough, and as to the system in force. It was also decided to invite the opinion of the managers of those schools at which no such Savings Banksare at present in operation as to the desirability of their being established.

- _ SCHOLARSHIPS. The School Management Committee recommend that 20 scholarships (5 for boys and 15 for girls), to the value of £5 per annum, together with free tulton and books, tenable for two years at the Secondary school, be offered to children between 14 and 15 years of age on the Ist August, 1905, who intend to become pupil teachers, and that the examination be conducted by the Head master and the teaching staff of the Secondary school on the 16th and 17th June next. AN UNSATISFACTORY EXPLANATION. A letter was submitted to the School Management Committee from the managers of the Warrington Parochial school, in reference to the comments contained in the recent reports by the Board of Education upon the boys' department, having particular reference to standards IV. VI. and VII. The explanations given by the managers were considered unsatisfactory, and instructions were given for a communication to be addressed to the teachers of the standards in question and to the managers, intimating that, although no further action will be taken in the matter on this occasion, the annual increments of salary in the cases of these teachers will be with-held in the event of any further complaints being received in regard to their ork.

FACILITIES FOR SWIMMING ASKED. The School Management Committee recommend that the Town Hall, Parks, and Baths Committee be requested to re-consider their decision not to entertain the applica- tion of the Education Committee to allow the free use of the second class swimming baths to children attend- ing public elementary schools or to inform the committee what facilities they are prepared to offer in this con nection.
'RE E T UIT CON.

At a meeting of the School Management Committe- it was resolved that a limited number of children, the circumstances of whose parents would otherwise pree clude their entering the school, be admitted to the- Secondary school free of charge (books also being provided), on the recommendation of the Head teachers and the Managers of the public elementary schools. The Committee also recommend that, in accordance with the conditions submitted, a limited number of scholarships, entitling the holders to free tuition at the Evening Continuation schools during two sessions, be awarded to children from the• public elementary schools, on the recommendation of the Head teachers of the Senior departments of those schools. The committee also resolved that in accordance with the conditions submitted, 15 scholarships, entitling the holders to free admission to the Technical Institute for one year and to the necessary books for an approved course of instruction, be awarded to each Boys' and each Girls', and 30 to each Mixed Evening Continoation szhool, the scholarships to be allotted on the result of an examination to be held at the end of the session, and to be renewable for not more than three years, provided a favourable report is received from the Principal of the Technical Institute.
NEW SCHOOLS. COMPETITIVE PLANS.

The Surveyor and the Director having reported to the Sites and Buildings Committee upon their inspec- tion of the specification received with the competitive plans for the new" Bolton " Council school, Latchford, the committee proceeded to consider the plans in ques- tion, and, after much deliberation thereon, it was resolved, that the plans bearing the distinguishing mark "Number 1" be adopted, and that their author be requested to submit an amended elevation for the approval of the committee. It was also decided that a fee of £l.O 10s., be paid to each of the four successful competitors. The competitive plans for the new " Beamont " Council School, Orford, were then opened, together with the envelopes containing the specifications, and the Surveyor and the Director were requested to con- sider and report upon them at a special meting of the Committee held yesterday.

div.head: February 286, 1905. CONGREGATIONAL UNION.
div.p: February 286, 1905. CONGREGATIONAL UNION.
ANNUAL MEETINGS IN LIVERPOOL.

The Rev. John Yonge and the Rev. H. Wall of War- rington, have been present at the annual meetings of the Lancashire Congregational Union held this week in Great George-street Chapel, Liverpool. They began on Tuesday evening, when the Rev. Dr. Ambrose Shepherd, of Glasgow, preached before a large congregation. On Wednesday morning the ministers and delegates met. The attendance was much above the average. The Rev. W. S. Rowlands (chorley) conducted the opening service. The Chairman's address was directed to a considera- tion of the circumstances of the "wonderful awatming of religious fervour and missionary zeal among the churches of the Principality." Did the Congregationalists of Lancashire, he asked, really want the revival to come their way? Were they anxious about the salvation of their unsaved brothers and sisters? Did they really believe in the Cross? Did its shadow even now fall across their path? "Do we see Christ the Son of the loving God abiding with us, lin our council chambers, our warehouses, our slums, in our individual lives, bearing our sins in His great heart ,of love, seeking to bear them away and lift us up to God? Are we willing to enter into vital fellowship with Him and live the crucified life? In the elder ages we read of abandonment in Christian service, utter- most surrender, a forsaking all and follow- ing, a counting all as so much dross, a willingness to be anathema from Christ for the sake of one's kinsmen according to the flesh." What was to hinder an awakening and ingathering such as Lancashire had never known heretofore? The revival of religious fervour and missionary zeal in their churches was the question which they were called upon to settle at these meetings No other question was comparable to it. A great opportunity was knocking at their Congrega- tional door, the opportunity of putting new life into their new constitution, the opportunity of exercising their freedom and going right to the front in missionary zeal and activity. And just behind the door stood God waiting to hear what response they were about to give and what consecration they were going to make. "He wants to use our churches for His great salvation, and if we are unwilling to be used He will pass us by, leav- ing us the poorer, and raise up other churches for the furtherance of His redeeming work. What is our answer to be ? " (Hear, hear). THE NEW CONSTITUTION.

On the recommendation of the Executive Committee a resolution was adopted accepting the new constitution of the Congregational Union of England and Wales as agreed upon at autumnal meetings held in Cardiff, September, 1901. The meeting also pledged itself to use every possible endeavour to make thenew constitu- tion operative and greatly useful. The persons nominated at the annual district meetings were appointed representatives of the Union on the General Council of the Congregational Union of Eng- land and Wales. EXAM-DUTTON SCHEME _ - - -

It was resolved, also on the recommendation of the Executive Committee—' That ministerial applicants for membership of the Union who have not previously held a pastorate or had special ministerial training shall be required to submit themselves to a scheme of examination provided by the Lancashire Union. This rule, however, shall not exclude exceptional cases being treated in an exceptional manner at the initiative of the Executive." LANCASHIRE COLLEGE.

The Rev. Dr. W. F. Adeney, Principal of the Lanca- shire Independent College, put before the meeting the claims of the College to the support of the several churches. He explained the changed position of the College now that it was attached to the Manchester University and its students could qualify for degrees in theology. These new conditions, he observed, both raised the standard and widened the platform of the College. Another step in advance had been drawing nearer to a sister college in Yorkshire. Under these circumstances, and remembering the ever-increasing need for a ministry thoroughly equipped to deal with present-day problems. Dr. Adeney appealed to the churches for generous support. The Rev. S. Pearson (Broughton Park) supported Dr. Adeney's appeal. SILCOATES SCHOOL.

Mr. J. A. Yonie (head master) called attention to the position of Silcoates Congregational School, now loca- ted at Saltburn-by-the-Sea, and Mr. J. Goodier (Haworth Manchester) explained a scheme for settling the school in its new abode by means of a limited company.

div.head: CENTENARY OF THE UNION.
div.p: CENTENARY OF THE UNION.

The Rev. T. Willis (general secretary) pointed out that in 1907 the centenary of the Lancashire Union will have been reached. It was unanimously agreed that the centenaty be celebrated in Manchester in the spring of that year, and that in connection with the celebration there shall be a memorial volume issued and a centenary memorial loan fund established. - -

In the afternoon there was a reception by the Lord Mayor and Lady Mayoress (Mr. and Mrs. John Lea) in the 'Town Hall. Among the delegates being Mrs. Yonge, Mrs. Walker and Nurse Whitfield all from Wycliffe Church, Warrington.

THURSDAY'S MEETINGS. THE EDUCATION QUESTION. The meetings were continued on Thursday in the George-street Chapel, Liverpool. The morning session was devoted to business, the making of grants in aid of various churches and mission stations that are not able to provide wholly for themselves, and so on. Mr. Henry Higson, of Blackburn, presided. PROGRESS OF THE CHURCH. The General Secretary (the Rev. T. Willis) presented his report on the work of the Unioa during the year. When the Union last visited Liverpool, fourteen years ago, there were, he said, including nine Welsh chapels in the Liverpool district, 305 Congregational places of worship in Lancashire, with accommodation for 156,480 persons. To-day, not including the nine Welsh chapels, the number was 320, with 162,616 sittings. Fourteen years ago there were seventy churches and missions aided by the Union. Last year grants to the amount of £2,490 were made to 74 churches and missions. Including the £2OO sent to the Church Aid Society, the grants last year were £2,690, but the contributions from the churches came short of this sum by £520. During 1904 new schools were opened at Garstang and Oswaldtwistle and new school-chapels at Pemberton, Clayton. Fairhaven, and Howe Bridge. The Chairman (as treasurer) presented his yearly balance-sheet, and both it and the secretiry's report were approved. Grants to the extent of £2,323 were agreed upon, and £2OO was voted to the Church Aid Society.

div.head: ELECTION OF CHAIRMAN.
div.p: ELECTION OF CHAIRMAN.

In the ballot for chairman for next year the three names that stood highest on the list were Mr. J. Boyle, of Bolton; Rev. W. Gough, of Bsrrowford ; and Rev. George E. Cheeseman of Ilnyton. Mr. Boyle asked to be excused. He appreciated the honour, but said that many others were entitled to be preferred before him and that he was unfitted for the position of chairman of the Union. Thereupon the Rev. P. K. Batchan (Heaton Moor) moved, the Rev. G. E. Cheeseman seconded, and it was resolved that Mr. Gough be chair- man for the year.

PROTEST AGAINST THE NEW EDUC. kTION ACTS I There was a short discussion on the education ques- tion, and the following resolution was adopted with complete unanimity : This Assembly of the Lanca- shire Congregational Union, remembering and re-affirm- ing the principles of national education, which it has all along professed, enters ' its renewed protests against the Education Acts of 1901 and 1903, ' and declares that it cannot accept as satisfactory any solution of the education question which does not I provide for complete and effective public control of all ; schools maintained out of the rates and taxes, which does not abolish sectarian tests and teaching, and which does not secure, in workable areas, local education authorities directly elected by popular vote. And this I Assembly will never consent to any proposal for the introduction into such schools during official school hours of sectarian teaching." ; The Rev. G. E. Cheeseman, who moved the resolution said it was generally understood that the next Parlia- ment was to be a Radical Parliament. What then were the minimum demands which Nonconformists expected ,to be granted? Well, in the resolution they had formu- lated their minimum; it was the irreducible quantity, the yen+ lowest that they would accept from any Government to he formed. These three things were insisted upon in the resolution. (1) Complete and efficient public con- trol of all schools that were publicly maintained ; (2) the abolition of all sectarian or ecclesiastical tests in a branch of the public service ; (3) the elimination from the school curriculum of all sectarian teaching. The first demand they put forward as citizens rather than as Nonconformists, the second was a demand for liberty of conscience for the teacher, and the third was a demand for liberty of conscience for the child. " That is our irredncible minimum. We will not accept from any party any measure of education which does not embody those three cardinal principles." (Applause). Two things gave him hope of victory in this matter, the unity of the Free Churches and the active co-operation of the Labour party. The Rev. J. Hirst Hollawell, in seconding the resolu- tion, said : "We ask for nothing for Nonconformists. We don't want a Nonconformist settlement. There is not a dogma of Nonconformity which we ask to have favoured, endowed, or propagated as part of the busi- ness of the State. We want an English policy, and not a Nonconformist policy. LICENSING REFORM. A resolution on the licensing question and pleading for the principle of local option was also passed, The Rev. David Evans. of Preston, gave an account of the religious awakening in Wales, and with this the meeting ended.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
Rugby Football.
(By " Ovalistr;

Last week's tame -display will make a return to cup tie excitements very welcome to-day. The second round should see Warrington still progressing, for though Keighley knocked out Salford on their own peculiar patch, their prospects at Warrington cannot be considered alluring. The difference between first and second division footballs was demonstiated in the Morecambe match, but there will not, of course, be the same disparity between to-day's teams. Keighley performed well all through the season, and only last week they trounced York by 23 points to 2 points, a feat which stamps them as an effective side. One of the Kingston Rovers men told me on Saturday that Warrington would find Keighley a difficult lot to beat, and there was no doubt the homesters will have to get their heads down in all seriousness for the occasion.

There is no uncertainty in Warrington as to the result of the tie, and the odds are unmistakably against the visitors. There has been one weakness in the home team, however, which has occasioned anxiety, and may do so to-morow. The fault is at half back where Hockenhall's absence continues tube severely felt. Thomas requires considerable practice before he becomes first-class, and the choice of partners for him is not very gay. J. Davies has had the misfortune to lose a brother in the Welsh Colliery accident, so he is out of the running for the present occasion. Isherwood shaped poorly last week, and the vacancy has gone to R. Bate. If the latter would smarten up his passes and movements generally he would be an excellent half, but slowness has hitherto been his bane. Both men must make an effort to get clear of the scrummage promptly and give passes which are not always anticiNted by the other side. The Warrington team will be as strong as possible bar Ffockenhall. The injured ones are pronounced fit again and Fish, Harris and Boardman will be heartily welcomed. The latter has been unfortun- ate in having two spells "on the club " this season. As a rule the "A. 8. of the team takes a lot of hurting. There is a possibility of Berry and Dickenson changing places, as the former is more used to right centre than left,and so far has not made much play for Fish. Dickenson is in good form just now and might be able to get the left winger going. There is no doubt that Warrington cannot afford to have the crack three- quarter standing idle in the neighbourhood of the touch-line.

By the way, speaking of Berry, the promising young centre must be careful ere he puts his foot to the ball when near his opponents' line. Last Saturday he put a cross-kick in when he might have gone on and scored, or at any rate have made a grand opening for Kenyon. There is nothing better than a cross- kick at the tight moment, but that moment is when the direct course to the line is blocked. A word in season to a persevering player like Berry should suffice. ---- , Warrington only just managed to scramble home against Hull Kingston Rovers on Saturday, and the exhibition of football was poor in the extreme. A gale of wind interfered with the course of the ball whether kicked or passed, but for two first-class teams the display was by no means creditable. Neither side appeared able to open out the game, and not a single try was scored. Warring- ton owed their win entirely to Preston's fine goal- kicking and Hallam's brilliant defence. The latter played his best game this season, while the famous forward for the second time scored all Warrington's points. This used to be a prerogative of Fish's ! The latter and Harris were both absentees, and this made considerable difference. Thomas and Isherwood were like oil and water behind the pack. They could not combine, and at half-time Isherwood gave way to Brookes. It was still evident, however, that Thomas must have an experienced half alongside if he is to he of any service in the position.

Broughton Rangers only got a point at Leeds, and have now practically left the duel between Oldham and Bradford, both of whom won. The game between the two on Monday at Oldham should decide the champions Lip as far as one game can do so. Bradford have lost the services of Dechan through injury, and the blow is a serious one at this stage or the proceedings. Warrington once more got ahead .of Wigan by the victory on Saturtlay,and I fancy they will finish the season in the first six. The struggle at the other end is getting deadly, and Batley by drawing at Salford, have made the position of St. Helens, Wakefield, and Swinton very precarious Runcorn are plainly booked for the wooden spoon, and ill-luck has certainly been theirs in plenty this season.

NOTES FROII KEIGHLEY.

The following is the team selected by the Keir,hley committee for to-day's Cup Tie :—Walker, back ; Jagger, Bateson, Crocker, and Stacey, three-quarters; Myers and Craven, half -backs ; Bradley, Blades, Bairstow, Tempest, Fearnley, McNicholas, Wilkinson, and Kilbey, forwards. This team is exactly the same that defeated Salford at Keighlev a fortnight ago, and it is practically identical with that turned Jut for the last six or seven weeks, during which period not one game has been lost, the last defeat sustained by the team being in the middle of ,Tanuary.

The side differs considerably from that which appeared at Warrington in the Senior Competition or First Division League last season, only one-third of the players then wearing the Keigliley colours being included in the team for to-day. Walker, Jagger,and Myers, in the back division, and Fearnley and Temppst, in the forwards, are the five old players. Of the new forwards Bradley and Blades are from the now defunct Holbeck club, and McNicholas is the old Leeds man. Keighley supporters are hoping that their men will be able to make a good fight at War- rington, but it would be going much too far to say that, generally speaking, victory is expected for the visitors even amongst their own friends.

-- - The team has no stars, because Myers is hardly a star nowadays, but it is made up of players of good, level ability, and is perhaps a safer con_bination than some more brilliant sets in the past. However, that may be, in the away matches this season there hos been no real evidence put forward that the team possesses any greater ability than before to win

div.head: INFLUENZA INCREASING
div.p: INFLUENZA INCREASING

div.head: Hockey. [By R.G.P.]
div.p: Hockey. [By R.G.P.]

After being idle for a fortnight Stockton Heath Ist eleven played New Brighton Wanderers at Grappenhan- road, and although being of course somewhat stale, and lacking the services of E. E. Woods, it was hoped that the home side would be able to account for the visitors. In the first half, the Wanderers had the sun and wind at their backs,and as the wind was high this told greatly in their favour. When half-time arrived the visitors were leading 1-0, a goal which ought not to have been allowed. There was a scramble in the Stockton Heath goal mouth, during which the referee was out on the touch line, somewhere about the home 25 line. The back who was playing the ball had his back to the referee, and being in a bending position, was therefore completely covering the ball, which never entered the net, being cleared. The Wanderers appealed for a goal, and the referee decided against the defending side despite appeals to the contrary. However the back who was playing the ball, says "It was over the line by about an inch."

The Stockton Heath forwards had been playing fairly well against the wind, and with luck R. Pierpoint would have scored with a shot which just went too high; while W. Richardson shot against the goal-keepers pads from close quarters, when a goal seemed certain. Turning round only " one down" as golfers say, the home team were fairly confident, and it was not long before the Stockton forwards were making their presence felt. Hereabouts the absence of L. Fairclough from the half- back line began to be felt, and with the halves later on falling away completely, the Wanderers had the better of the exchanges, and eventually ran out victors I by 3-0.

The England v. Wales match at Cardiff proved some- what of a farce, as the northern section of the Welsh team refused to play at the last moment, and con- sequently 10 Newport players were called upon. As it was England won by 6-0, but it was more the fault of the muddy ground, than the efforts of their opponents' that kept the score within normal bounds. A great deal of jealousy exists between the southern and the northern sections of the Welsh Hockey Association, but it will need a good deal of 'explanation to justify such an unsportrnanlike act, as to bring players from all parts of England, and then to treat them in this manner.

Owing to the bad weather several matches were abandoned, but of those played Sale and Bowdon drew a very even match, the score being one all. Timperley defeated Alderley 2 0, while Kersal drew with Altrincham, and Huyton just managed to defeat Sefton.

This week the Stockton Heath Club play their return match with Timperley, when the following will repre- sent Stockton Heath :—First (at home) : R. G. Pier- point, goal ; E. Pierpoint and E. E. div.head: SCHOOL CONCERT IN THE PARR HALL.
div.p: SCHOOL CONCERT IN THE PARR HALL.

An unusually pleasing spectack was presented at the Parr Hall on Thursday, by the pupils of Miss Lloyd Williams. Lorne House School. The building was filled with a large audience who frequently and heartily' expressed their pleasure at the efforts of their enter- tainers. The principal feature of an excellent pro- gramme was a cantata "Red Riding Hood" in which the principal characters were Misses E. Cook (Red Riding Hood), A. Oakley (wolf). and E. Winstaniei (principal fairy). The singing and speaking of the children was splendid and a particularly pleasing feature was the introduction of a dance by some 213 little girls attired as fairies In fact throughout tho evening the children acquitted themselves in a manner which reflected great credit upon the tuition of Miss Williams; song's in character and an action song were given by the senior girls, while ths song and chorufl "The Tardy Scholar" by Miss M. Rigby and a °home was heartily encored. A similar tribute was paid to the Misses Houghton and Kisby (trained by Miss Spinks) for a Welsh dance. "Afternoon tea " was well sung by the Misses A. Whalley' And H. Hawell. Miss D. Perdu was recalled for a pianoforte solo whilst Miss M. Whitmore met with equal success in a coon song "Go bye bye" in which she was assisted by a chorus in character costume. The playing of the band in the march "La Marseillaise" and a waltz was excellent, their efforts being warmly received. Miss T. Tanner was successful in a song "Hungry Army." Several selections were given by chorus composed of the pupils, in an admirable manner. The Misses Phar and Walker were responsible for a well played mandoline duet, "Cromartie," while the Misses Walker and Jones were heartily applauded for the duet "Flow 'on thou shining river." Miss Snelling sang sweetly "Japanese love song" and the Misses E. Pickup, L. Turner, and C. Titchett were encored for a song and dace "Pit pat." Miss lloscollar acted as accompanist.
