Mr. Warburton having resigned the office of treasurer, Mr. Yorke was elected to succeed him. THE FEDERATION MEETING. The Secretary presented a report of the proceedings at the half-yearly meeting of the Lancashire and Cheshire [Federation of Trades and Labour Councils, when several !matters of importance, including Corporation contracts I clauses, were discussed. THE QUESTION OF A CANDIDATE. CORPORATION OFFICIALS' SALARIES. IMr.BUCKLEY reported on the proceedings at the last meeting of the Warrington Labour Representation Com- , mittee.Councillor Wright,he saidtpresented a report on the f proceedings of the Town Council, dealing more particu- larly with his stand in regard to the increase of Corpora- • tion officials' salaries. He had opposed each one in turn, from the workingman's point of view, believing that it was not right that increases should be given to the officials when they had so many underpaid workmen in the employ of the,Corporation. (Hear, hear.) Some ,of the men were receiving 18s. per week and even less j than that, and it was outrageous to think of raising the ' salaries of higher officials an. to to take no notice of i such cases as he mentioned. The committeo endorsed Councillor Wright's action as being the only ,w can stand a Labour candidate could take under the circum- A. ce stances. It was evident to him (Mr. Buckley) that froro their two Labour members needed more assistance. from They would have to create a commotion in the Town Council, and to clear out some of the "old women and political tricksters." It was all very well for the local For i Press and ottmr people to say that a man's abilities 1, 1 ought to be considered. It appeared to him judging '-', y, from recent events that abilities were not considered 1 4,4 and that it was a question of favouritism. Apart from 1 " that, they did rent want to consider .1, man's abilities only, but to think of what was a living , wage, and it was an impossibility for any workingman to live on 18s. per week. An important item introduced was the question of a Parliamentary Labour candidate. The matter had been quiet for the past few weeks, but it had now cropped up again, and he, as secretary, had been instructed to keep on applying ' for a Labour candidate for Warrington. Councillor STOTT said that SOOle of the delegates were of the opinion that the Corporation workmen who were under-paid ought to make some effort to try and improve their conditions by organizing and making a formal application for increases. Be did not think any able-bodied Corporation employs ought to receive less than 245. per week and he would like to have that fixed as the minimum rate. If the men did not make an effort for themselves it would be said that they were satisfied. The report was accepted. HELP FOR THE BLIND. The Council passed a resolution in support of the Bill which is being promoted by the League of the Blind with the object of obtaining state aid for those who are handicapped by loss of their eyesight. THE FAIR WAGES CLAUSES. The SECRETARY said nothing further had been done with regard to the Corporation fair wage clauses, but a meeting would probably be held at an early date, as he had mentioned the matter to the Town Clerk. The CHAIRMAN said that some time ago he urged the Trades Council to arrange a demon- stration of protest against the action of the Town Council, but his suggestion was not accepted. It seemed to him that the time spent in drafting the clauses had been wasted. Was the Council going to take the matter "lying down," without raising its voice? He asked the members to bestir themselves and do something to enforce the clauses which were passed just before the November elections and rescinded directly afterwards. Mr.YorexE said that unless some pressure was brought to bear, it appeared to him that the clauses would lapse. Councillor STOTT said he did not think the Trades Council would obtain satisfaction from the clauses that would eventually be submitted, and it would be for them to take action then. He was absolutely certain they would not get the clauses they had before. A proposal to hold a demonstration of protest against interference with the clauses was not supported,and the meeting concluded.

(Cricklewood).—ln reply to your further letter, you are incorrect when you state that I men- tioned an exceptional case when I referred to the six seta of ivory balls, which, by the articles of agreement, have to be provided for the Robert Stevenson match in May, in order to avoid, if possible, having to play with foul balls. This provision is constantly made when ivory balls are used. If you want another instance the following one will servp :—Lancashire met Yorkshire just three weeks ago in one of the rounds of the Inter-County Championship. Three games of 500 up were _played, and no less than four different sets of ivoi7 balls were used during the day owing to one or other of the balls not running true; and unfortunately for the players the last set were worse than the first set. Such a thing cor Id never have occurred with Crystalate balls. These bT :Is being a mechanical mixture and not an animal grow. b, are of exactly the same density and specific gravity all the way through, and therefore being thus quite free from any bias, must run perfectly true on a tame table. Lieutenant-Colonel Alderson (Ipswich), The screw- back mentioned by you is a great stroke, but is, of course, quite possible, especially if tried a good few times. When playing ordinary long in-offs into top pockets from the D, it is much better to play them as half-ball strokes without side. If the in-oil be narrow even from the end of the D, then check side should be used and running side if it be wide. C.A.R. (York).—I am very glad that you can so fully endorse the various points given in my article on Screw, which appeared last week. I shall be glad to hear from you again. Re your question as to the best height above the bed of the table to place incandescent lights. lam not quite sure about this. I have electric lamps over my own table, and these give the best and most even light placed about 33 inches from the bed of the table, and I should imagine the same height would be most suitable for incandescent gas lamps. RISO LEVI. HOCKEY. • STOCKTON HEATH v. NEW BRIGHTON WANDERERS. Played at Gmppenhall-road. The visitors started with the sun and wind at their backs,but for along time even play resulted. At length M'Clelland set his forwards on the move, and from a scramble in the Stockton goal mouth the referee awarded the Wanderers a goal. Half- time score : Wanderers, one; Stockton, nil. Upon turning round and having the elements in their favour,' the Stockton Heath team seemed sure•victors. From the bully off C. R. Bond put in a good run. The Stock- ton halves however fell away in a very disappointing manner, and with the visitors taking full advantage of this weakness, it was not long before Tomlinson scored with a hot shot. Again New Brighton attacked and 'Batty getting through had no difficulty in adding num- ber three. Final score :—New Brighton, three; Stock- 'ton Heath, nil. The story goes that Lord Stanley's refusal of the post of Chief Secretary for Ireland was in these words : , "I'd rather sit naked on a nest of wasps." KNEW FOURTEEN LANGUAGES.—The death has occurred at St. Annes-on-the-Sea of Mr. Frank Thomas 'teacher of modern languagesat the Blackburn Technical School: The deceased had a thorough knowledge of ' fourteen languages, including Russian, Chinese, and Dutch. He was formerly in business at Manchester, I where he was often in request as interpreter in the law courts.
